nodes.title: Change behaviour by changing how understood the child feels, not by tightening control
nodes.description:
The book's founding goal, restated by the revision through the behaviour-analyst lens rather than through a contrast with control. The mechanism is unchanged — a child whose experience is understood behaves in ways that begin to make sense — but the revision arrives at it by way of observation rather than assertion, and it fences the promise: connection is not claimed to change behaviour overnight, and boundaries stay in place.

Sources:
- "To look for patterns. To ask what might be happening beneath behaviour instead of reacting only to what I could see."
- "Instead of asking only, How do we stop this behaviour? I learned to ask, What is this child trying to tell me or accomplish?"
- "And I began to understand that connection is not a luxury in parenting. It is the foundation from which regulation, resilience, and trust can grow."
- "That doesn't mean connection magically changes behaviour overnight. It doesn't mean we stop setting boundaries, or that parenting suddenly becomes easy."

nodes.title: Build a predictable rhythm inside your own walls to replace the village you don't have
nodes.description:
The goal the Personal Note sets up, and the revision keeps its premise and its constraint intact while cutting the passage that restated them. The isolation diagnosis stands — no grandparents nearby, no circle of adults, a house that can feel like an island — and so does the answer: the village is not recoverable, but a rhythm inside the house is. What the revision drops is the "returning to a steady center" language; what replaces it is a plainer formulation of the same idea as returning, done inside hours that are already full.

Sources:
- "Without grandparents close by or neighbours who truly know our kids, the house can quickly feel like an island."
- "We may not be able to recreate the village exactly as it once was. But we can build a rhythm inside our own walls."
- "It is about noticing what is already happening inside the hours you have and using some of those moments differently."
- "It is about returning."

nodes.title: The recurring confession at the kitchen table: "It's just us"
nodes.description:
Herman grounds the book's problem statement in a moment she says repeats across hundreds of parents she has sat with. The absence of nearby grandparents and neighbours who know the children turns the household into an island with no circle of adults to share the load. She states this holds whether the home has two parents or one. This is the premise that makes an in-house rhythm necessary rather than optional.

Sources:
- "Over the years, I’ve sat across from hundreds of parents at kitchen tables, in school"
- "It’s just us."
- "Without grandparents close by or neighbours who truly know our kids, the house can quickly"

nodes.title: Margins are razor-thin, so "connecting" registers as one more chore
nodes.description:
The second constraint on the method is time. When every hour is already spoken for, an instruction to connect lands as another to-do item rather than as a foundation. This observation is what forces the method to be short and embedded in existing hours instead of additive. It directly constrains the design of the touchpoints.

Sources:
- "But the margins are razor-thin. When every hour is already accounted for, trying to "connect" can feel like another chore to check off a to-do list rather than the foundation that keeps us grounded."
- "trying to "connect" can feel like another chore to check off a to-do list rather than the"

nodes.title: Parenting's loudest noise is the parent's own self-doubt
nodes.description:
The opening line locates the difficulty not in the child's volume but in the parent's interior. The revision softens the claim from an absolute to a tendency — self-doubt "can scream" rather than "screams" — and it drops the old reassurance that the reader is "not failing", replacing a verdict on the parent with a description of what they are doing.

Sources:
- "Nobody prepares you for how loud parenting actually feels."
- "It's not just the literal noise of a chaotic house; it's the volume of the emotions spinning out of control, and how loudly your own self-doubt can scream at you when you're just trying to figure out what to do next."
- "If you are reading this, I want you to hear me: You care deeply. You love fiercely. And chances are, you are doing far more than anyone sees."

nodes.title: The question under 'how do I fix this behaviour?' is 'what is this child trying to tell me?'
nodes.description:
The revised Personal Note reframes the founding question. Where the earlier draft asked why a difficult moment feels so hard to understand, the revision states the reframe as a professional habit the author brought to parenting: stop asking how to stop a behaviour and start asking what the child is trying to accomplish with it. This is the hinge the whole method turns on, and it now arrives with its own method attached — a set of questions the author asks before deciding what a behaviour means.

Sources:
- "Instead of asking only, How do we stop this behaviour? I learned to ask, What is this child trying to tell me or accomplish?"
- "What happened before this? What changed afterward? What does this child move toward or away from? What seems to bring relief? What am I missing?"
- "I learned that words are only one source of information. When a child is overwhelmed, upset, or dysregulated, they may not have access to the words that accurately explain what is happening for them."

nodes.title: Reach for another strategy, another system for controlling behaviour, another list of shoulds
nodes.description:
The rejected path, restated in the revision. The earlier draft named it as tightening control, adding consequences or trying harder; the revision names it as the shape the method refused to take — one more system, one more list. It is rejected twice over: once by the author's own experience of having the knowledge and still finding that something was not working, and once by the method's self-description.

Sources:
- "Not as another system for controlling behaviour."
- "Not as another list of things parents should be doing."
- "And what might my child need from me that I wasn't going to find simply by reaching for another strategy?"
- "I had knowledge. I had experience. I had spent years helping other families understand their children. And still, something wasn't working."

nodes.title: Solve it with more time — more hours in the day with your child
nodes.description:
The rejected option, and the revision moves where it is stated. The Personal Note's line about not needing more hours in the day is cut, but the identical claim survives untouched in the retained "About the RootedInGood™ Method" section, which is now the only place the front matter rules the option out. The Personal Note carries the same constraint in a different register: nothing may be added to an already full plate.

Sources:
- "The RootedInGood™ Method is built around a simple but powerful idea: meaningful connection doesn't require more time; it requires intention."
- "It is about being intentional without adding more to an already full plate."
- "When every hour is already accounted for, trying to "connect" can feel like another chore to check off a to-do list rather than the foundation that keeps us grounded."

nodes.title: Be intentional inside the hours you already have, without adding to a full plate
nodes.description:
The endorsed posture, and the one everything downstream implements. The revision keeps the constraint that made it viable for the reader it recruited — nothing is added to the plate — and defines the work as noticing what is already happening and spending some of those moments differently. The method is named as a return rather than an addition.

Sources:
- "It is about being intentional without adding more to an already full plate. It is about noticing what is already happening inside the hours you have and using some of those moments differently."
- "It is about returning."
- "But as a way of returning to the relationship underneath all of it."
- "We may not be able to recreate the village exactly as it once was. But we can build a rhythm inside our own walls."

nodes.title: The method's founding pick: return to the relationship underneath, rather than reach for another strategy
nodes.description:
The Personal Note's decision, restated by the revision. It is made at the point where professional knowledge ran out — the author had the theory, the experience and the track record, and her own child still did not respond — and it resolves toward the relationship rather than toward a better technique. The revision gives the decision its own line: theory must bend to real life.

Sources:
- "Theory must bend to real life."
- "The RootedInGood™ Method began to take shape in that intersection where professional knowledge met personal humility."
- "But as a way of returning to the relationship underneath all of it."
- "And then one of my own children began struggling in ways that didn't respond to the strategies I knew. That was humbling."

nodes.title: Practise the three short daily touchpoints: Focused Support, Intentional Listening, Physical Connection
nodes.description:
The method overview names the concrete practice: three short daily touchpoints the parent performs. The front matter states their purpose as supporting the child's nervous system while strengthening the relationship, and leaves the mechanics to the chapters. It also sets expectations for how the practice is carried out — returning to it quickly rather than executing it flawlessly.

Sources:
- "At the heart of the method are three short, daily touchpoints designed to support your"
- "child’s nervous system while strengthening your relationship:"
- "is meant to be lived, not mastered or perfected, but practiced in real time. You will not"

nodes.title: Connection becomes the foundation regulation, resilience and trust grow from
nodes.description:
The payoff the Personal Note claims, and the revision states it more carefully than the earlier draft did. Connection is called a foundation rather than a luxury, but the claim is immediately fenced: it is not promised to change behaviour overnight, it does not replace boundaries, and it does not make parenting easy. What it provides is something to come back to.

Sources:
- "And I began to understand that connection is not a luxury in parenting. It is the foundation from which regulation, resilience, and trust can grow."
- "That doesn't mean connection magically changes behaviour overnight. It doesn't mean we stop setting boundaries, or that parenting suddenly becomes easy."
- "It means we have something solid to return to."

nodes.title: The parent stops reacting out of urgency and starts responding with steadiness
nodes.description:
The parent-side result claimed in the method overview is a changed experience of hard days rather than their removal. Herman says the method builds resilience that carries into tense moments and changes how those moments feel from the inside. The concrete shift is from urgency-driven reaction to steadiness, plus having predictable ways to return after disconnection.

Sources:
- "carries into the tense moments. It changes the way you experience them. Instead of"
- "reacting out of urgency, you begin responding with steadiness. Instead of feeling"
- "disconnected, you create predictable ways to return."

nodes.title: Use the method to change someone else, or to correct your co-parent
nodes.description:
The personal note lists this as an explicit non-goal. Herman states flatly that the work is not about changing anyone else and not about correcting a co-parent. The instruction is to lead honestly and let steadiness do the talking rather than to apply the method to another adult.

Sources:
- "It is not about changing anyone else."
- "It is not about correcting your co-parent."
- "Let your steadiness speak."

nodes.title: Chase a polished outcome
nodes.description:
The third named non-goal is performance. Herman rules out pursuing a finished, presentable result, consistent with the later statement that the method is lived rather than mastered or perfected. Neither parent nor child is expected to move through it flawlessly.

Sources:
- "It is not about chasing a polished outcome."
- "is meant to be lived, not mastered or perfected, but practiced in real time. You will not"

nodes.title: Keep the scope strictly to you and your child, right where you are
nodes.description:
The endorsed scope is a single relationship. Herman frames the whole undertaking as the reader's own journey and confines it to the parent-child pair. If others notice a change later, the instruction is simply to let them in rather than to recruit them into the work.

Sources:
- "As you begin, I want you to hold one important truth: This is your journey."
- "It is about you and your child."
- "Stay focused on the relationship you are building right where you are. Lead honestly."

nodes.title: Settle what the work is for before starting: your relationship, not anyone else's behaviour
nodes.description:
Before any technique, the personal note asks the reader to fix the scope. Three candidate purposes are named and refused — changing others, correcting a co-parent, chasing a polished outcome — and one is affirmed. Herman presents this as a truth to hold at the outset, which makes it a precondition rather than an afterthought.

Sources:
- "As you begin, I want you to hold one important truth: This is your journey."
- "It is not about chasing a polished outcome."
- "It is about you and your child."

nodes.title: Work through the companion RootedInGood Toolkit: worksheets, guided pages, tracking
nodes.description:
For readers who want structure, a separate paid-or-optional companion resource exists with worksheets and guided pages. The front matter presents it as suited to parents who enjoy writing, reflecting and tracking progress. It is offered but pointedly not required.

Sources:
- "If you are someone who finds comfort in structure, there is a separate companion"
- "The Toolkit offers optional worksheets and guided pages for parents who enjoy writing,"

nodes.title: Read the book alone and let the four markers meet you where you are
nodes.description:
The default path needs no pen and no pause in reading. The book carries four recurring markers — Root and Reflect, Rooted Reminder, Rooted in Practice, Rooted Anchor — described as invitations rather than assignments, checklists or tests. Herman says the book stands on its own and contains the full rhythm, philosophy and practical application.

Sources:
- "They are invitations, not assignments. Some parents process quietly and internally."
- "Root and Reflect is your invitation to look inward."
- "You do not need it. This book stands on its own. It contains the full rhythm, philosophy,"

nodes.title: The book chooses the pen-free path and makes the Toolkit strictly optional
nodes.description:
Presented with two ways to do the reflective work, the front matter names the book-alone path as sufficient and demotes the Toolkit to a preference for a certain learning style. Herman closes the point with a principle rather than a logistics note: worksheets are not where connection starts. The choice keeps the entry cost at zero, consistent with the razor-thin-margins premise.

Sources:
- "You don’t need a pen, and you don’t need to stop reading. Just let them meet you right"
- "You do not need it. This book stands on its own. It contains the full rhythm, philosophy,"
- "begins in small, intentional moments."

nodes.title: Authority claim, rebuilt: Under the Umbrella Tree, a career begun at nineteen, and a lineage of mentors
nodes.description:
The revision replaces the short credential paragraph with a full professional history, and shifts what the authority rests on. The earlier bio led with titles and totals; this one leads with a disposition — curiosity — and traces where it came from. The centre is named for the first time (Under the Umbrella Tree), the founding age moves from twenty to nineteen and gains its setting (teachers college, a social skills programme run out of her father's Tai Chi studio), and the credentials are made specific: Registered Behaviour Analyst and Ontario Certified Teacher. The 1,000 children figure survives but is now qualified by breadth of presentation rather than volume alone.

Sources:
- "Lolly Herman is a Registered Behaviour Analyst and Ontario Certified Teacher, founder of Under the Umbrella Tree, speaker, mentor, and mother of three."
- "Lolly's professional career began at nineteen, while she was still in teachers college and running a small social skills program after school and on weekends out of her father's Tai Chi studio."
- "Over the course of her career, Lolly has personally supported more than 1,000 children and their families across an extraordinary range of needs, personalities, abilities, challenges, and circumstances."
- "That breadth of experience has shaped the lens she brings to parenting: Behaviour may look the same from one person to the next, but careful observation can help us look beneath what we see and beyond what we hear, before deciding what it means."

nodes.title: The method's origin: her own child didn't respond to the strategies she already knew
nodes.description:
The personal half of the authority claim. The revision moves it out of the bio and into the Personal Note, where it now sits at the end of the curiosity narrative rather than standing as a credential. The structure is the same — expertise met a child it could not explain — but the revision states the humbling plainly and lets "theory must bend to real life" carry the conclusion.

Sources:
- "And then one of my own children began struggling in ways that didn't respond to the strategies I knew."
- "That was humbling."
- "I had knowledge. I had experience. I had spent years helping other families understand their children. And still, something wasn't working."
- "Theory must bend to real life."

nodes.title: Scope limit: not a substitute for medical, psychological or therapeutic care
nodes.description:
The Gentle Disclaimer draws the boundary around everything the method claims. It supports connection, communication and emotional understanding inside the parent-child relationship, and nothing more; it does not diagnose or treat. Where distress exceeds what the parent can hold alone, the book routes the reader to a qualified professional and frames that referral as strength rather than failure.

Sources:
- "It is not a substitute for medical, psychological, or therapeutic care, and it is not"
- "intended to diagnose or treat any condition."
- "Asking for support reflects strength."

nodes.title: Build a steady daily rhythm of connection with your child in about nine intentional minutes
nodes.description:
The chapter's governing aim is not a behaviour fix but a rhythm: a short, repeatable daily commitment that shifts how parent and child experience each other before anything visible changes. The author frames the reader's starting point as safe and un-graded, so the goal is approachable from wherever the relationship currently stands. The whole chapter hangs off this promise that a small commitment produces a large relational impact.

Sources:
- "Nine intentional minutes a day can begin to shift how you and your child experience each other-not as a quick fix, but as a steady rhythm that strengthens trust where it matters most."
- "You are not here to be evaluated, graded, or given a list of impossible parenting standards. You are here to build a steady rhythm with the child you love."

nodes.title: Run all three touchpoints daily: Focused Support, Intentional Listening, Physical Connection
nodes.description:
The full form of the method is three named moments of connection woven into an ordinary day, totalling nine minutes. The author insists this is a rhythm rather than a program, schedule or additional task, and that it flexes rather than being tied to a clock. This is the option the chapter presents as the method proper.

Sources:
- "At its heart, this method is about three simple moments of connection woven into your day. They're short. They're doable. And they can make a lasting impact."
- "Not a program. Not a schedule. Not another thing on your to-do list. It’s a rhythm you can trust."

nodes.title: Start smaller: two minutes, or just one of the three touchpoints
nodes.description:
The chapter offers a reduced entry point for parents in a season of disconnect, where nine minutes feels foreign or hard. Rather than requiring the full rhythm on day one, it permits a single touchpoint or two minutes and expects the practice to grow on its own. This is presented as a legitimate way in, not a lesser version of the method.

Sources:
- "Nine minutes of intentional connection might feel hard, or even foreign, especially if you're in a season of disconnect with your child."
- "Start with just two minutes, or with just one of the three touchpoints. Let it build naturally from there."

nodes.title: Commit to the rhythm at whatever size you can hold today
nodes.description:
The chapter asks the parent to choose an entry point rather than to choose between doing the method and not doing it: full nine minutes, or a smaller slice that builds. Both are endorsed, because the chapter's claim is about consistency of return rather than volume. The sum is stated flatly as the commitment being asked for.

Sources:
- "That’s it. Just nine intentional minutes."
- "A rhythm you can return to, no matter what kind of day you’re having."

nodes.title: Focused Support (2 minutes): step in gently before your child becomes overwhelmed
nodes.description:
The first touchpoint is pre-emptive rather than reactive. The parent intervenes with help at the point before overwhelm arrives, which places it upstream of the behaviour the parent might otherwise be managing. It is budgeted at two minutes.

Sources:
- "Focused Support"

nodes.title: Intentional Listening (5 minutes): let your child feel fully heard without fixing or teaching
nodes.description:
The longest of the three touchpoints requires the parent to set distractions aside and withhold the instinct to correct or instruct. The stated deliverable is the child's felt experience of being heard, not the resolution of whatever they are describing. Five minutes is the allotted share.

Sources:
- "Intentional Listening"

nodes.title: Physical Connection (2 minutes): offer closeness, comfort or calm so they know they are safe
nodes.description:
The third touchpoint is bodily rather than verbal: closeness, comfort or calm offered as a reminder of safety and love. Its purpose is stated as reminding the child of something already true rather than teaching them anything new. Two minutes completes the nine.

Sources:
- "Physical Connection"

nodes.title: The trust and bond hold, and connection stops costing nine minutes
nodes.description:
The chapter predicts that the rhythm eventually becomes self-sustaining: parents who keep returning to it find that feeling connected no longer depends on clocking the minutes. The explanation offered is that what has been built together persists. Connection is described as accumulating through repetition rather than arriving in a breakthrough.

Sources:
- "once you're on the other side of this, you may find that it doesn't even take nine minutes a day to feel connected anymore."
- "Why? Because the trust, the bond, and the rhythm you've built together begin to hold."
- "It happens in dozens of small, steady ones."

nodes.title: The author's curveball: a son whose behaviour no one, including her, could explain
nodes.description:
The method's origin story, and the revision expands it from a paragraph into the chapter's spine. The author is a behaviour specialist, a centre founder and a present mother, and none of it lets her read her own child. The revision keeps the original admission — she was right there and still could not see it — but adds what she could not see, so the story now has a resolution rather than only a wound.

Sources:
- "Which is why, when one of my sons began struggling in ways no one could quite explain, it shook me to my core."
- "There were outbursts. Emotional overwhelm. Behaviour that didn't make sense. Not to his teachers, not to other professionals, and, hardest of all, not to me."
- "I wasn't missing it. I wasn't distracted. I was right there."
- "And still, I hadn't been able to see what was underneath it."
- "That was my curveball. That's where this story really begins."

nodes.title: One child needed far more for years, and the guilt of dividing herself settled in
nodes.description:
The author describes a long season, measured in years rather than weeks, when one of her three children required more co-regulation, presence, advocacy and energy than the others. She carried a low-level guilt about fairness and whether her other children felt unseen. This story is what sets up the equity question the chapter then answers.

Sources:
- "There was a long season in our home when one of our children needed far more than the others. Not for a week. Not for a month. For years."
- "I worried about fairness and whether the others felt unseen, convinced that the only way to be a good parent was to make sure everyone got the exact same piece of me."

nodes.title: Equality: give every child the same amount of time
nodes.description:
The chapter names splitting yourself into identical shares as the approach many parents assume is required, and the author admits she held it herself. It is defined precisely so it can be set aside. The chapter treats the pressure behind it as self-imposed rather than coming from the children.

Sources:
- "Equality was trying to give each child the same amount of time."
- "the pressure I was carrying wasn’t coming from my children; it was coming from me. From an unspoken belief that good parenting meant dividing myself perfectly."

nodes.title: Equity: respond to each child's actual needs with a responsive presence
nodes.description:
The alternative the chapter endorses is matching presence to real need rather than to a fair-share formula. In a multi-child home the rhythm is said to weave rather than multiply, so a season weighted toward one child is described as wise responsiveness rather than neglect of the others. The target is responsive presence, not equal minutes.

Sources:
- "Equity was responding to each child's actual needs."
- "In a home with multiple children, rhythm doesn't multiply. It weaves. The goal is not equal minutes. It's responsive presence."

nodes.title: Choose equity over equality when more than one child is in the house
nodes.description:
The chapter presents this as an explicit either/or and picks a side. The author reports it as the realisation that changed her, arriving after years of silently weighing her children's shares against each other. Some seasons are said to require more in one direction without that meaning anyone else is unseen.

Sources:
- "It was never about equality. It was about equity."
- "Some seasons require more from you in one direction. That doesn't mean the others are unseen. It means you are responding"

nodes.title: Look for micro-moments: small intentional pivots already in your day, not grand gestures
nodes.description:
The equity principle is worked out through tiny schedule adjustments rather than special events: leaving early for ice cream before practice, picking up something simple from the dollar store, lingering in the car after a drop-off. The Recap turns this into the chapter's first Try This instruction, aimed at pivots already present in the day rather than newly planned ones. The author is explicit that these small moves were sufficient.

Sources:
- "Leaving ten minutes earlier to grab an ice cream with one child before practice. Picking up an extra activity at the dollar store so there was something simple waiting for us at home. Lingering in the car a little longer after a drop-off with one child."
- "Not grand gestures. Just small, intentional pivots. They were enough."
- "Look for Micro-Moments: Instead of planning grand gestures, notice the small, intentional opportunities for connection already happening in your day."

nodes.title: The guilt lifted and creativity came back once she stopped chasing equal minutes
nodes.description:
The reported result of abandoning equal division is a release of the parent's own pressure rather than any immediate change in the children. The author describes a softening, and creativity returning inside that softening. This is the chapter's evidence that the equity shift pays the parent first.

Sources:
- "That shift released me. When I stopped chasing equal minutes, something softened. And in that softening, creativity returned."

nodes.title: The inner voice saying "this just isn't us" means unfamiliar, not failing
nodes.description:
The chapter anticipates the parent's scepticism in their own words and reframes it. Connection is said not to feel natural at first, particularly after a long tense stretch, and unfamiliarity is explicitly separated from ineffectiveness. This caution is what makes the smaller entry point defensible instead of a retreat.

Sources:
- "You might find your own inner voice whispering things like: This isn't going to work. They're not going to respond to fist bumps or notes from me. This just isn't us."
- "But just because it feels unfamiliar doesn’t mean it isn’t working. Resistance doesn’t mean failure. It means you’re trying something new."

nodes.title: You are your child's co-regulator: you help set the tone and create the conditions
nodes.description:
The chapter's Rooted Reminder, restated with the parent's control over the outcome dialled down. The revision changes "you set the tone" to "you help set the tone" and "you create the conditions for connection to grow" to "conditions in which connection can grow" — the parent shapes the environment rather than producing the result.

Sources:
- "You are your child's co-regulator. That means you help set the tone. You shape the environment. You create conditions in which connection can grow."

nodes.title: Vignette: a mom brushing her daughter's hair while she told her about a dream
nodes.description:
The first of the chapter's connection vignettes, and the revision reassigns it. In the earlier draft this was the author's own morning with her own daughter; the revision hands it to an unnamed mom, moving it into the same reported-by-other-parents register as the rest of the set. The content is unchanged: a few minutes of ordinary presence that grounded both of them.

Sources:
- "One morning, a mom found connection in the simplest gesture: brushing her daughter's hair while she told her about a dream from the night before. Those few minutes of presence grounded them both."

nodes.title: Vignette: a dad's strongest connection came on the drive to soccer practice
nodes.description:
This story deliberately strips away the features parents assume connection requires: eye contact, a prepared talk, any pressure on the child. What remains is undivided listening in a car going somewhere else. It doubles as a picture of Intentional Listening in a real setting.

Sources:
- "A dad once shared that his strongest moment of connection happened during the drive to soccer practice. No eye contact. No pressure. Just undivided listening."

nodes.title: Vignette: a mom sitting silently beside her son while he built Lego after school
nodes.description:
Connection here involves no conversation at all, only the parent entering the child's activity on the child's terms. The absence of questions and agenda is the point of the story. It shows presence functioning without any verbal exchange.

Sources:
- "For one mom, it looked like sitting silently beside her son while he built Lego after school. No questions. No agenda. Just showing up in his world."

nodes.title: Vignette: a caregiver's weekly note left on her child's pillow
nodes.description:
A repeated small ritual, not a conversation, that the child began to anticipate. Its value in the chapter is the predictability — the child came to look forward to it — which mirrors the rhythm argument. It also answers the imagined objection about notes not landing.

Sources:
- "Another caregiver described a weekly ritual of leaving a small note on her child’s pillow, something her daughter came to look forward to."

nodes.title: Treat the method as behaviour management: fixing, compliance, an easier-to-manage child
nodes.description:
The rejected reading of the method, and the revision fences the core belief that grounds the rejection. "It's not the child's fault" is kept but immediately qualified, so the reframe no longer reads as a claim that behaviour carries no limits or consequences. The chapter now separates where you begin from what you enforce.

Sources:
- "This method isn't about "fixing" behaviour. It's not about compliance or making your child "easier to manage.""
- "If there is one core belief that has shaped every year of my work with families, it is this: It's not the child's fault."
- "That doesn't mean behaviour has no limits or consequences. It means we begin by remembering that children are still developing the skills we are asking them to use."

nodes.title: Let it all slide because you're connected now: drop limits in favour of warmth
nodes.description:
The other rejected option, stated so the method cannot be read as permissiveness. The revision softens the supporting claim from a guarantee to a capacity — limits "can provide" safety rather than "give them a sense of" it — and drops "to thrive" from the assertion that children need boundaries.

Sources:
- "Leaning into these three daily touchpoints does not mean you stop setting limits or holding firm boundaries. This isn't a "let it all slide because we're connected now" approach."
- "Children need boundaries and consistent guidance. Limits can provide safety, predictability, and trust. What the RootedInGood™ Method changes is how we try to help those boundaries land."

nodes.title: Use connection to cushion boundaries so limits land as protection
nodes.description:
The endorsed posture keeps both: the parent leads with love and still says no. Connection is said not to erase boundaries but to change how they are received by a child who feels seen, heard and safe. Finding the nine minutes is framed as making the relationship a safe place for rules to land, not as surrendering authority.

Sources:
- "Connection doesn’t erase your boundaries; it cushions them."
- "You can lead with absolute love and still say no."
- "When you start finding those nine minutes, you aren't losing your lead as a parent. You are making your relationship a safer place for your guidance to land."

nodes.title: Refuse the connection-versus-boundaries choice: use connection to make limits land
nodes.description:
The chapter explicitly declines the either/or it has just laid out, rejecting both compliance-chasing and limit-dropping. Connection is positioned as the instrument that makes boundaries clearer, kinder and more effective as time passes. The parent's job is named as co-regulating and modelling safety rather than controlling.

Sources:
- "This method is not about choosing between connection and boundaries. It’s about using connection to make your boundaries clearer, kinder, and more effective over time."
- "And part of our job is not simply to control what we see on the outside, but to remain curious about what may be happening underneath it—to co-regulate, model, guide, set boundaries, and create the kind of connection in which growth can happen."

nodes.title: Limits get easier to hear when the relationship underneath them feels secure
nodes.description:
The outcome the boundaries section claims, and the revision meaningfully lowers it. The earlier draft promised the child would not experience limits as rejection but as protection; the revision claims only that limits can be easier to hear and tolerate without feeling like the relationship has been withdrawn. The parent's guidance gets "a safer place to land" rather than a guaranteed reception.

Sources:
- "Connection doesn't erase your boundaries; it cushions them. When your child feels seen, heard, and safe with you, limits can be easier to hear and tolerate without feeling like a withdrawal of your relationship."
- "In my own home, I've found that my kids are far more willing to hear a hard "no," accept a limit, or take in feedback when the relationship underneath it feels secure."
- "When you start finding those nine minutes, you aren't losing your lead as a parent. You are making your relationship a safer place for your guidance to land."

nodes.title: Remember: children aren't problems to solve, they're people to understand
nodes.description:
The chapter's closing line, and the paragraph beneath it is where the revision does its most careful work. The earlier draft made two flat developmental verdicts — the six-year-old who should have known better genuinely didn't, the teenager who needs to calm down genuinely can't. Both are cut. In their place is a description of capacities that develop over time, and a job description for the parent that keeps boundaries in it: not simply to control what is visible, but to stay curious about what is underneath while still guiding and setting limits.

Sources:
- "Children are not born knowing how to regulate emotions, handle disappointment, or process the intensity of their inner world. These capacities develop over time, through experience, maturation, guidance, and support."
- "They're still learning. And part of our job is not simply to control what we see on the outside, but to remain curious about what may be happening underneath it—to co-regulate, model, guide, set boundaries, and create the kind of connection in which growth can happen."
- "Children aren't problems to solve. They're people to understand."

nodes.title: Try This: take a breath check-in and drop your shoulders before the next transition
nodes.description:
The Recap's second Try This asks the parent to release physical tension in the moment just before a daily transition with the child. It echoes the chapter's opening instruction, which asked the reader to breathe and let their shoulders drop before starting at all. It is the one practice aimed at the parent's own body rather than at the child.

Sources:
- "Take a Breath Check-In: Before stepping into your next daily transition with your child, pause for a moment. Let your shoulders drop and notice what you are bringing into the interaction."
- "Before we step into these pages, take a breath and let your shoulders drop."

nodes.title: Regulate your own nervous system before trying to co-regulate your child
nodes.description:
The chapter's governing aim is that the parent learns to manage their own internal state first, treating calm not as a bonus but as the precondition for every other move in the method. Lolly frames this as the system behind every parenting moment. The goal is not flawless composure but a working ability to tend one's own nervous system so it can be offered to the child. Everything else in the chapter hangs off this.

Sources:
- "Before you can co-regulate with your child, you have to regulate yourself. You cannot give what you don’t have."
- "This chapter is about learning how to take care of the system behind every parenting moment: your own nervous system."
- "Calm comes first. Always. It is not an afterthought or a luxury; it is the absolute prerequisite for helping a struggling child."

nodes.title: Core premise: you cannot model calm from a dysregulated nervous system
nodes.description:
The chapter's founding premise is a capacity argument — a depleted or activated parent has nothing regulated to transmit. Lolly reaches it only after admitting she could steady other people's children at work while losing her footing at home, which she attributes to overwhelm rather than indifference. She separates knowing the tools from being able to use them under load. This premise is what makes self-regulation a prerequisite rather than a preference.

Sources:
- "You cannot model calm from a dysregulated nervous system. And you cannot create a connection when your internal world is running on fumes."
- "I knew the tools. I taught the tools. But knowing the science and living the science are two very different things."
- "I wasn’t snapping because I didn’t care. I was snapping because I was overwhelmed and exhausted, carrying the invisible weight so many parents carry."

nodes.title: Vignette: the Tuesday morning when Lolly saw she was escalating her son, not calming him
nodes.description:
A named vignette anchoring the chapter. Running late, with one child unable to find shoes and another crying over a bowl, Lolly barked directions at the son who struggled most with self-regulation and then registered the fear underneath his behaviour. She describes her own body's rise — chest tightness, heat, racing thoughts — and recognises his stiffness and shallow breath as her dysregulation mirrored back. The realisation is that her intensity was fuelling his.

Sources:
- "It was a Tuesday morning. We were already running behind."
- "It was like watching my own dysregulation reflected at me in real time. My intensity was feeding his."
- "At that moment, I realized something painful but honest: I wasn’t co-regulating him. I was escalating both of us."

nodes.title: Your nervous system is the thermostat: children read your body through neuroception
nodes.description:
The chapter's mechanism claim. Children scan the parent biologically rather than consciously, picking up jaw tension, movement pace, tone beneath words and the energy carried into a room. Because their bodies read the parent's body before hearing any words, the parent's state sets the room's temperature: steadiness settles the child, overwhelm pushes them toward protection mode. Crucially the chapter insists this state is changeable rather than fixed personality.

Sources:
- "Through a process called neuroception, children pick up on:"
- "Their bodies read your body before they ever hear your voice. When you’re steady, your child feels steadier. When you’re overwhelmed, their system often goes into protection mode."
- "Your calm is not a personality trait. It is a nervous-system state, and states can change."

nodes.title: Autopilot: shut down big emotions, demand obedience, move to consequences
nodes.description:
The posture the chapter sets aside. It describes an inherited default — rules learned in the parent's own upbringing that were about compliance rather than connection — surfacing as shutting emotions down, demanding obedience, or jumping to consequences. The chapter is careful not to shame this: it names it as a nervous system replaying old learning. But it treats it as a habit that can be questioned and stopped rather than passed forward.

Sources:
- "So if your first instinct is to shut down big emotions, demand obedience, or move quickly to consequences, that doesn’t mean you’re a bad parent."
- "It means your nervous system is replaying what it learned long before you ever had a child of your own."
- "Many of us also grew up with unspoken “rules” about children and emotions, rules that were more about compliance than connection."

nodes.title: Notice the rise early: track the body's whispers before the outburst
nodes.description:
The approach the chapter endorses. Regulation is said to begin long before any outburst, in small bodily signals — tightening shoulders, shallow breath, fast thoughts, anger or numbness — that mark the nervous system leaving its window of tolerance. Noticing earlier is what buys the parent a choice. The chapter explicitly reframes the aim as awareness rather than perfection.

Sources:
- "It starts in the moments your body whispers:"
- "These are early signals. Signals that your nervous system is rising out of its window of tolerance. The earlier we notice the rise, the sooner we can soften it."
- "This is why self-regulation matters so deeply. It isn’t about being perfect. It’s about becoming aware. Awareness is the beginning of everything."

nodes.title: Choose your response instead of reacting on autopilot
nodes.description:
The chapter puts a genuine choice to the parent between two named paths: the inherited reaction pattern and a noticed, chosen response. It grants that the old pattern is not a moral failing while insisting it is not binding either. The decision is framed as ongoing and daily rather than one-time — deciding which habits come forward into your parenting and which stop with you.

Sources:
- "Once you can notice yourself, you can choose your response instead of reacting on autopilot."
- "You get to decide which ones come forward into your parenting, and which ones stop with you."
- "You are not bound by how you were raised or how you reacted yesterday. You get to choose differently."

nodes.title: Map your state on the 5-point awareness scale, watching for Level 3
nodes.description:
The chapter's named tool: a five-level scale Lolly uses with families, running from Calm & Grounded through Slightly Activated, Rising Tension, Dysregulated, to Overloaded, each with body-and-mind markers and a matching move. Level 3 is flagged as the starred early warning and the cue to pause and support yourself before escalation. The chapter explicitly disclaims the goal of living at Level 1; the point is catching the rise sooner. It also asks the parent to practise this during ordinary moments — car rides, cooking, before school pick-up.

Sources:
- "Below is a 5-point scale I use with families to map out these internal shifts."
- "Pay close attention to Level 3-this is your early warning sign. Hitting a 3 is your cue to pause and support yourself before the situation escalates."
- "Important Reminder: The goal isn't to stay at a Level 1 all day. It’s simply to notice the rise sooner so you can return with clarity."

nodes.title: At Level 3: roll shoulders, unclench hands, one long exhale
nodes.description:
The scale's prescribed move for Rising Tension, the level Lolly stars as the early warning. The body markers given are tightening shoulders, a clenching jaw, shallowing breath and speeding thoughts. The response is deliberately small and physical — three quick adjustments that can be done without leaving the room or announcing anything. It is the cheapest intervention in the chapter because it is taken earliest.

Sources:
- "My shoulders tighten. My jaw clenches. My breath becomes shallow. My thoughts speed up. This is my early warning sign."
- "Early Warning: Roll shoulders, unclench hands, one long exhale."

nodes.title: At Levels 4 and 5: say "I need a moment", then step away safely
nodes.description:
The scale's moves once the rise has passed the early warning. At Level 4 — racing heart, flooding, interrupting, snapping or shutting down — the instruction is to stop talking, name the need aloud with a set phrase, and ground with a hand on the heart and feet on the floor. At Level 5, overloaded and possibly yelling or withdrawing, the chapter directs the parent out of the room entirely, with cold water and fresh air. Both treat leaving as legitimate rather than as failure.

Sources:
- "Stop talking. Say: "I need a moment." Hand on heart, feet on floor."
- "Step away safely. Splash cold water on your face and get fresh air."
- "I feel out of control, panicked, or emotionally flooded. I may yell, withdraw completely, or feel unable to recover without space."

nodes.title: Run the Breathe-Name-Anchor reset when you cross into Level 3 or 4
nodes.description:
The chapter's named three-step sequence, offered as something to try immediately and triggered by the scale reading. Breathe is one long deliberate audible exhale; Name is silently identifying the emotion without judgment, with sample wordings given; Anchor is a hand on the chest, feet felt on the floor, and a reminder to slow your own system before entering the child's. It is designed to be run in place, wherever the parent is standing.

Sources:
- "Whenever you feel yourself crossing into Level 3 or 4, pause exactly where you are and run through this sequence:"
- "Name: Silently identify the emotion without judgment (“I am flooded right now” or “I am completely overwhelmed”)."
- "Anchor: Place a hand on your chest, feel your feet on the floor, and remind yourself: I should slow down my own system before I step into theirs."

nodes.title: Lolly's thirty-second reset: leave the room, hand on heart, "Slow down, Lolly"
nodes.description:
What Lolly actually did on the Tuesday morning, and the lived prototype of the reset sequence. She stopped, left the room, put a hand on her heart, took one long shaky breath and spoke a private script to herself prioritising her calm over her instructions. She measures the cost precisely — under thirty seconds. Returning, she changed her posture rather than her demands: kneeling, softening her voice, making her body smaller, slower, safer, and offering to sit with him.

Sources:
- "So I did something I'd never done at home before. I stopped. I walked out of the room. I put a hand on my heart. And I took one long, shaky breath."
- "It took less than thirty seconds, the same time it takes to fill a glass of water."
- "I knelt next to him. Softened my voice. Made my body smaller, slower, safer. “It’s a hard morning, hey? I’ll sit with you and help if you need.”"

nodes.title: He got dressed — because she changed, not because he did
nodes.description:
The reported result of the thirty-second reset. Within a few minutes the boy dressed himself with no bribes, threats or consequences held over him. The chapter is precise about the causal direction: nothing about the child or the scene had changed when she walked back in, and he was not suddenly calm. What changed was her state, which gave him somewhere to settle.

Sources:
- "In just a few minutes, no bribes, no threats, no 'consequences' hanging over his head, he actually got dressed."
- "When I walked back in, everything felt different. Not because he had changed; he was still on the floor in the same pyjamas, but because I had changed."
- "It wasn’t that he was suddenly perfectly calm; it was just that my own calm gave him a safe place to land."

nodes.title: The quiet fear: "If I soften, will my child still listen to me?"
nodes.description:
The chapter surfaces an objection it says many parents carry silently, sometimes as frustration and sometimes as fear, and states it as a direct question in a reflect box. It places the question at exactly the point where a parent begins refilling their own system and regaining footing. Naming it lets the chapter answer it head-on rather than leaving softening to read as permissiveness.

Sources:
- "an important truth often rises to the surface, one that many parents carry quietly, sometimes with frustration, sometimes with fear:"
- "“If I soften, will my child still listen to me?”"

nodes.title: Self-regulation strengthens boundaries rather than weakening them
nodes.description:
The chapter's answer to the softening fear, stated as a claim about what a steadier system makes possible: firm limits held with less yelling, less panic and less shame. Lolly reports it from her own home, and attributes her children's respect for boundaries to the connection and unwavering presence she has built — explicitly crediting connection rather than treating it as a cost paid against authority.

Sources:
- "self‑regulation doesn’t weaken your boundaries; it strengthens them. When your nervous system is steadier, you can hold firm limits with less yelling, less panic, and less shame."
- "my children are more likely to respect a boundary because of the connection and unwavering presence I’ve built with them, not despite it."

nodes.title: Caution: a depleted system makes regulation harder, and you deserve support too
nodes.description:
A deliberate caveat against reading the chapter as pure willpower. It lists real loads — caring for aging parents, raising a neurodivergent child, a demanding job, invisible emotional burdens, anxiety or depression — and concedes that under them regulation can feel impossible, because the parent is a human being with a human nervous system. It then lists warning states (numb, constantly irritable, checked out, overwhelmed, unable to come back down) and directs the parent outward for help.

Sources:
- "If your system is depleted, regulation will feel harder, sometimes impossible. Because you’re a human being with a human nervous system."
- "Please know this: You deserve support, too."
- "Reaching out to your doctor, therapist, partner, or a trusted friend is not a weakness. It is wisdom."

nodes.title: What you focus on you see more of: the pink elephant and the yellow car
nodes.description:
A principle about attention offered as the bridge from inner awareness to outward posture. The chapter uses two everyday illustrations — being told not to think of a pink elephant, and noticing yellow cars everywhere once one is pointed out — to argue that the mind amplifies whichever lens it looks through. The practical consequence is that deliberately shifting the lens toward connection and gratitude changes how the child and the day appear.

Sources:
- "It’s the same phenomenon that happens when someone says, “Don’t think of a pink elephant.” Suddenly, that’s all you can picture."
- "Our minds are wired to amplify whatever lens we are looking through."
- "When you begin shifting your lens toward connection and gratitude, your entire view of your child and your day transforms."

nodes.title: Vignette: Lolly's dad — "Today is all you have. That's why they call it the present"
nodes.description:
A short childhood vignette Lolly credits to her father, which she says planted itself deep and grew alongside her. The lesson is temporal: yesterday's learning is behind you, tomorrow is not promised, and the only moment actually lived in is this one. She applies it directly to hard parenting moments as an instruction to take one small step forward rather than staying knotted up.

Sources:
- "My dad taught me a lesson when I was very young, one that planted itself deep and grew alongside me."
- "He used to say, “Today is all you have. That’s why they call it the present.”"
- "And if you find yourself standing in a hard moment, take one small step forward. Return to connection. Return to presence."

nodes.title: Vignette (Before): the kitchen mess, and bringing the storm into the room
nodes.description:
The first half of the chapter's paired Before & After scene. Arriving home to dishes, open cupboards, crumbs and paint supplies, the parent's chest tightens and the instinct is to yell, itemise the mess and demand to know who is responsible. Voice sharpens, movements speed up, and the storm arrives before the parent notices carrying it. The children's responses are catalogued — shrinking, eye-rolling, disappearing, tears — and the spiral is described as predictable whenever the parent's system is in survival mode.

Sources:
- "Your instinct is to yell. To point out the mess. To demand to know who left the milk out and why no one cleaned up."
- "The kids shrink. One rolls their eyes. One disappears down the hallway. One bursts into tears."
- "The moment spirals exactly the way it always does when your nervous system is in survival mode."

nodes.title: Kitchen (After): pause at the edge of the mess and open with genuine curiosity
nodes.description:
The replayed scene with the regulated response. The parent pauses before entering, feels the same chest tightness but reattributes it to their own exhaustion rather than the children's failure, breathes, lowers volume and leads quietly, with a self-statement about choosing how to show up. Then comes the chapter's named script — a curiosity question instead of an accusation — followed by an appreciative line and an invitation to clean up together.

Sources:
- "..But this time, you pause at the edge of the mess and choose your response. You feel the tightness in your chest, but you recognize it for what it is: your own exhaustion, not their failure."
- "“Wow, it looks like a lot happened here. What were you working on?”"
- "You smile. “Okay. I love the creativity. Let’s clean this up together so we can enjoy the rest of our night.”"

nodes.title: The predictable spiral breaks and the kids respond to stability, not threat
nodes.description:
The reported result of the curiosity opening. Children show their work — a half-painted cardboard jet, attempted muffins, a Lego castle — and what rises in the parent is connection rather than tension. The chapter tallies the outcome concretely: the kitchen is cleaned, nobody leaves crying, and the parent walks away with evidence that grounding is their strongest tool. It generalises this as presence shifting the atmosphere and calm inviting cooperation.

Sources:
- "And just like that, the predictable spiral is broken. The kids respond to your stability, not to a threat."
- "The kitchen gets cleaned, no one leaves the room crying, and you walk away with the ultimate proof that your centred grounding is the greatest tool you have."
- "Presence shifts the atmosphere. Calm invites cooperation."

nodes.title: Try This: map your warning signs and use the Breathe-Name-Anchor reset
nodes.description:
The Recap's two assigned practices. The first is mapping where tension hides in your body during ordinary daily routines, deliberately before it converts into a sharp reaction. The second is running the named reset when tension rises — one long exhale, silently naming the feeling without judgment, hand on the chest to ground. Together they pair the diagnostic with the intervention.

Sources:
- "Map Your Warning Signs: Notice where tension hides in your body during daily routines before it turns into a sharp reaction."
- "Use the Breathe-Name-Anchor Reset: When tension rises, take one long exhale, silently name the feeling without judgment, and place a hand on your chest to ground your system."

nodes.title: Remember: not flawless calm, but noticing your state and finding your footing again
nodes.description:
The Recap's closing claim and the chapter's redefinition of success. Self-regulation is reframed as a recovery skill — noticing sooner and returning — rather than never losing your cool, with repair explicitly counted as teaching the child as much as regulation does. What the parent's micro-shifts install in the child is a belief about the parent's steadiness under difficulty. The chapter names this steady system as the root of co-regulation and the heart of the method.

Sources:
- "Self-regulation isn’t about flawless calm; it’s just about noticing your state and finding your footing again. Your unwavering nervous system is your child's safest place to land."
- "It’s about noticing sooner and returning. Your child learns just as much from your repair as from your regulation."
- "“My parent is settled and calm, not just when things are easy, but when things are hard.”"

nodes.title: Be the regulated presence your child borrows until they can self-regulate
nodes.description:
The chapter's aim is for the parent to become the steady nervous system a dysregulated child can lean on, so that co-regulation becomes the bridge to the child's eventual self-regulation. The parent is not trying to stop the storm but to be shelter inside it. Everything else in the chapter — the postures, scripts and touchpoints — serves this single capacity.

Sources:
- "It is the moment your steady calm meets your child’s chaotic storm, creating a bridge where dysregulation ends and deep connection begins. You are not here to control the weather; you are here to be the shelter."
- "Now that you’ve seen how co-regulation forms the vital bridge to your child’s self-regulation, we can begin peeling back the layers on how to bring this to life inside your daily calendar."

nodes.title: Core premise: co-regulation is your calm helping create their calm, not a script or technique
nodes.description:
The chapter's definition, with the mechanism restated more carefully in the revision. The earlier draft said children borrow the parent's breath and voice because it is how they learn to self-regulate and cannot do it until we do it with them; the revision drops the dependency claim and keeps the accumulation one — repeated experiences of co-regulation help a child gradually build their own capacity.

Sources:
- "At its core, co-regulation is the process where your calm helps create their calm. It's not a script or a technique."
- "These repeated experiences of co-regulation help children gradually build their own capacity for self-regulation."

nodes.title: Self-regulation develops gradually across childhood and keeps maturing into early adulthood
nodes.description:
The chapter's developmental premise, and the single place the revision most visibly pulls back. The author supplied two versions of this chapter and asked the reviewer to choose; the later one removes every hard number and every absolute verdict. "Around age 7 or 8" and "into the mid-twenties" become gradual development into early adulthood. "They don't actually know better yet" becomes a distinction between knowing and being able to access what you know. "Misbehaviour is often a biological inability, not a choice" — the strongest claim in the earlier draft — is replaced with a child who may know exactly what is expected and still not reach it while overwhelmed. The function is unchanged: the parent's presence is necessary rather than indulgent. What changes is that the chapter no longer diagnoses.

Sources:
- "Self-regulation develops gradually across childhood and adolescence, and even then, it can be uneven and highly dependent on support, stress, temperament, development, and context."
- "The brain systems involved in emotional regulation continue maturing into early adulthood."
- "So when your six-year-old falls apart at the grocery store, remember: knowing what to do and being able to do it in an overwhelmed moment are not the same thing."
- "When your teenager slams their door and spirals instantly, what looks like defiance may also be a sign that they're in over their head."
- "A child may know what is expected and still struggle to access that skill when overwhelmed."

nodes.title: Stay near and emotionally available while the child moves through the storm
nodes.description:
The posture the chapter endorses: remaining physically close and emotionally open without trying to end the feeling. It is explicitly not permissive — boundaries hold, but they are held without escalation. The book presents this as a different way of standing your ground rather than an absence of one.

Sources:
- "It’s staying near and emotionally available while they move through the storm, showing them, again and again, that they’re not alone in it."
- "Boundaries still matter. It’s not permissiveness; it’s just a different way of standing your ground. Co‑regulation is how you hold them without escalating the moment."

nodes.title: Rush in to rescue, fix the situation, or force immediate compliance
nodes.description:
The chapter names this cluster of instincts explicitly in order to set it aside: rescuing the child from the feeling, fixing things so the crying stops, or demanding compliance on the spot. It also rejects the related move of isolating a child and instructing them to calm down. These are the default reactions the method asks the parent to notice and decline.

Sources:
- "Co-regulation is not about rushing in to rescue your child from their feelings, nor is it about fixing the situation at all costs just to make the crying stop. It is not about forcing immediate compliance"
- "not by being isolated and told to calm down, but by borrowing your strength until they can stand on their own."

nodes.title: Let the rules slide so the moment stays calm
nodes.description:
The second posture the chapter refuses: reading emotional availability as permission to drop limits. The book is emphatic that softening presence does not mean softening boundaries. It heads off the misreading that co-regulation equals permissiveness.

Sources:
- "it is definitely not about letting the rules slide."
- "Boundaries still matter. It’s not permissiveness; it’s just a different way of standing your ground."

nodes.title: Choose connection before correction in the hard moment
nodes.description:
This is the chapter's decisive turn: in the moment of dysregulation the parent chooses presence over rescue, fixing, compliance or rule-dropping. The author states the rule twice — once in the closing anchor and again in the Recap — and illustrates it as what co-regulation looks like in practice. Every practice that follows in the chapter is downstream of this one choice.

Sources:
- "Connection must always precede correction. Your presence is the bridge they cross to find their own calm."
- "That’s what co‑regulation looks like in real life: choosing connection before correction, and staying close long enough for your child to learn how to stand on their own."

nodes.title: Sit beside a crying child without trying to stop the tears
nodes.description:
The simplest enactment of the chosen posture: stay physically alongside and let the crying run its course. The parent does nothing to shorten the feeling. The chapter offers it as one of three concrete forms presence can take.

Sources:
- "Sometimes that means sitting beside a crying child without trying to stop the tears."

nodes.title: Name the feeling without trying to make it go away: "You’re really frustrated right now. I get it."
nodes.description:
A scripted move the chapter supplies verbatim. The point is that naming is not a step toward removing the emotion — the feeling is acknowledged and allowed to stand. It pairs acknowledgement with the parent staying put.

Sources:
- "Sometimes it’s naming a feeling without trying to make it go away: “You’re really frustrated right now. I get it.”"

nodes.title: Step away to settle yourself, then come back in — "part of the return"
nodes.description:
The chapter licenses the parent to leave the moment briefly when they cannot bring calm to it. It pre-empts the guilt reading by insisting this is not a failure of co-regulation but an act of it. The return is treated as the substantive part.

Sources:
- "And sometimes, it means recognizing that you need a moment to settle yourself before coming back in to support them."
- "That’s not failure."
- "It’s part of the return."

nodes.title: Say "I’m struggling too, but I’m here" on the days you have nothing polished to offer
nodes.description:
An honest-presence script for the exhausted or frustrated parent. The chapter attaches it to its reframe that co-regulation needs a willing moment rather than a good day. The child's requirement is closeness and warmth, not composure.

Sources:
- "Sometimes, that presence might sound like: “I’m struggling too, but I’m here.”"
- "Co-regulation does not require a flawless parent or a picture-perfect day. It begins with a single, willing moment."
- "They need you to be close. To be warm. To show them that mistakes and messiness don’t scare you away"

nodes.title: The three daily touchpoints from Chapter 1 give co-regulation a place to live
nodes.description:
The chapter connects back to the three touchpoints introduced earlier and clarifies their relationship to co-regulation: they are containers, not substitutes. Each brief moment is described as supporting the child's nervous system in real time. This is the hinge between the chapter's principle and its daily mechanics.

Sources:
- "Back in Chapter 1, you were introduced to the idea of three daily touchpoints that form the heart of the RootedInGood™ Method."
- "Each touchpoint, though brief, is designed to do more than connect. It supports your child’s nervous system in real time, helping them feel grounded, seen, and safe."
- "The touchpoints don’t replace co‑regulation; they give it a place to live."

nodes.title: Touchpoint #1 — Focused Support (2 minutes): step in before overwhelm peaks
nodes.description:
The parent offers physical or task help early, before frustration crests, rather than waiting for the collapse. The signal being sent is stated explicitly by the book. Two minutes is the stated duration.

Sources:
- "Touchpoint #1: Focused Support (2 minutes)​ Sends the signal: You’re not doing this alone. It’s when you gently step in to help before your child becomes overwhelmed, showing them you’ve got their back."
- "Focused Support (2 mins): Offer physical or task help before frustration peaks so they know they aren't alone."

nodes.title: Touchpoint #2 — Intentional Listening (5 minutes): distractions away, no solving
nodes.description:
Five minutes of emotional space in which the parent listens without judging, correcting or problem-solving. The chapter is specific that distractions are put aside and the problem is left unsolved. Being fully heard is the whole deliverable.

Sources:
- "Touchpoint #2: Intentional Listening (5 minutes)​ Offers emotional space to process, without judgment or correction. It’s when you put distractions aside and let your child feel fully heard, without trying to solve the problem."
- "Intentional Listening (5 mins): Put away distractions and listen closely without trying to make it right, judge, or correct."

nodes.title: Touchpoint #3 — Physical Connection (2 minutes): restore the baseline of safety
nodes.description:
Two minutes of closeness, warmth or quiet proximity, positioned for after long or emotionally charged stretches. Its function is restorative rather than corrective. The Recap lists a hug, gentle touch or quiet closeness as the forms it can take.

Sources:
- "Touchpoint #3: Physical Connection (2 minutes)​ Restores a sense of safety and comfort, especially after a long or emotionally charged day or moment."
- "Physical Connection (2 mins): Offer a warm hug, gentle touch, or quiet closeness to restore a baseline of safety."

nodes.title: For neurodivergent or more sensitive children the process is slower — "The goal isn’t speed. It’s safety"
nodes.description:
A caution placed directly after the touchpoints: the same practice will look different and take longer for some children, and the chapter marks that as acceptable rather than as a shortfall. It resets the success criterion away from how quickly a child settles. This guards the touchpoints from being run as a stopwatch exercise.

Sources:
- "And for neurodivergent children or those with more sensitive nervous systems, this process may take longer and look different, and that’s okay."
- "The goal isn’t speed. It’s safety."

nodes.title: Vignette: the mom who waited by the front door with a granola bar and a smile
nodes.description:
A mother the author worked with had a daughter who unravelled after school into tears, defiance or shutdown. Instead of correcting, she met her at the door with food and a smile, and often they did not talk at all. The book uses her as its clearest picture of presence without agenda.

Sources:
- "One mom I worked with shared how her daughter would often unravel after school; tiny things would trigger tears, defiance, or shutdown."
- "Instead of jumping in with corrections, she started waiting by the front door with a granola bar and a smile. They didn’t talk at first."
- "That’s co‑regulation. Not an answer. A presence."

nodes.title: The wordless after-school welcome hardened into a ritual that said "you don’t have to have it together"
nodes.description:
What the mother's repeated presence produced: a predictable soft landing the daughter could count on. The chapter reports it as something that formed over time rather than worked immediately. Its message to the child is stated in the book's own words.

Sources:
- "But over time, that soft landing became a ritual."
- "It said, "You don't have to have it together right now. I'm here."

nodes.title: Vignette: the Birthday Party Anchor — the author staying at her son's drop-off parties
nodes.description:
During a season when loud, socially complex birthday parties overwhelmed her son, the author stayed even when the invitation said drop-off. She positioned herself as an anchor rather than a hovering intervener — a soft nudge, a shared look across the room, or simply being close enough to be glanced at. Her reason was her read of his nervous system, not distrust of him.

The revision connects this scene to the chapter's new opening. The same parties that used to get a pep talk beforehand are now the ones she attends, and a line is added that names the switch explicitly: she stopped asking whether he knew what to do and started watching what helped him use what he already knew. The shared look across the room is the same gesture the chapter opens with.

Sources:
- "Even when the invitations said “drop-off party,” I often stayed."
- "Not because I didn't trust him, but because I understood his nervous system."
- "So I stayed nearby, acting as an anchor when things started to tip. I wasn't hovering or intervening unless I needed to."
- "I had finally stopped asking whether he knew what to do and started paying attention to what helped him use what he knew."
- "Sometimes it was a soft nudge. Sometimes it was a shared look across the room."

nodes.title: He stayed longer, recovered faster, needed fewer prompts — staying was not holding him back
nodes.description:
The reported result of the author's sustained anchoring across many parties. Confidence grew precisely because he was supported while still learning, rather than pushed into independence early. The author names her own realisation that proximity created room to grow.

Sources:
- "Over time, those parties began to feel different. He stayed longer. He recovered faster. He needed fewer prompts. And slowly, his confidence grew, not because he was pushed into independence before he was ready, but because he was supported while he was still learning."
- "I remember realizing that staying wasn’t holding him back. It was giving him the space to grow."

nodes.title: The child learns their feelings don't drive you away, and begins to seek you out
nodes.description:
The chapter's long-run outcome, with the revision loosening both the trigger and the guarantee. The earlier draft made the turning point a child who lets you share space without pushing you away; the revision makes it a child who experiences you as steady even when the kind of closeness they need changes — which allows for the child who does push away. "What will make them start seeking you out" becomes "can help them begin to", and the reason shifts from safety felt instinctively to a presence that has become familiar through repetition.

Sources:
- "When your child begins to experience you as a steady presence in hard moments -even when the kind of closeness they need changes-that's the beginning of a rhythm."
- "Over time, just being there with them in the mess is what can help them begin to seek you out."
- "They don't do it because of a rule; they do it because your presence has become familiar, safe, and steady."

nodes.title: Try This: practice the three daily touchpoints — 2 min, 5 min, 2 min
nodes.description:
The Recap's assignment converts the chapter's principle into a daily routine of three timed moments. It restates each touchpoint as a concrete instruction for the parent to run. This is the chapter's only prescribed practice task.

Sources:
- "Practice the Three Daily Touchpoints:"
- "Focused Support (2 mins): Offer physical or task help before frustration peaks so they know they aren't alone."
- "Physical Connection (2 mins): Offer a warm hug, gentle touch, or quiet closeness to restore a baseline of safety."

nodes.title: Remember: a flawless parent isn't required — only a safe, regulated presence to land inside
nodes.description:
The Recap's closing line restates the chapter's rule and its reassurance in one sentence. It joins the ordering principle (connection first) to the standard of performance (not perfection). It is the line the chapter wants carried forward.

Sources:
- "Connection must always precede correction. Your child does not require a flawless parent; they just need a safe, regulated presence to land inside."

nodes.title: Anchor yourself so you meet hard moments with connection instead of control
nodes.description:
The chapter's stated aim is not to change the child first but to change the adult's presence. It asks the parent to notice how they show up before reaching for any behaviour strategy, so that when the child escalates the parent is centred rather than reactive. Presence is framed as the medium in which regulation becomes possible at all.

Sources:
- "This chapter is about anchoring yourself, so that when the waves come (and they will), you’re centred enough to meet them with connection instead of control."
- "Before we focus on changing our child’s behaviour, we start by noticing how we show up. Presence is the soil where regulation grows."

nodes.title: Core premise: the child feels the parent before they hear the parent
nodes.description:
The chapter opens with its governing claim: tone, body energy and eye contact reach the child ahead of any sentence. Words are not dismissed, but they are placed second to the felt signal. This premise is what makes the rest of the chapter's instruction coherent, since it means presence is doing the work that parents assume their wording is doing.

Sources:
- "Your child feels you before they hear you."
- "The tone of your voice, the energy in your body, the way your eyes meet theirs… these are the signals that shape how safe and seen they feel in the moment."
- "Long before your words land, your presence does. That’s where connection is built… or subtly eroded."

nodes.title: Vignette: the author's season of snapping, when tone said more than words
nodes.description:
Lolly describes a stretch of her own parenting where the sentences she used were defensible but the delivery was not. Tense shoulders, a clipped tone and exhausted sighs carried the real message, and her child received it. She reports the realization stung most when she was trying hardest to do it right, and that noticing it in herself let her see the same pattern in other parents.

Sources:
- "The words I said weren’t cruel; they were technically fine. But the way I said them? That was another story."
- "The tension in my shoulders, the clipped tone, the exhausted sighs… they said more than my words ever could. And my child heard them loud and clear."

nodes.title: Vignette: the basketball coach whose good intentions crushed the author's son
nodes.description:
Her 11-year-old son made a respected, high-pressure competitive team. The coach was loud and urgent rather than cruel, told the parents outright that he tailored his toughness to what each child needed to perform, and put her son on explicit warning. The approach worked for many kids on that roster. The chapter uses it as its central case of a gap between intention and impact: care that was genuine still landed as pressure.

Sources:
- "“I treat kids the way I think they need to be treated to perform,” he told us."
- "“He’s on a tight leash,” the coach admitted. “If he missteps, shows frustration, or has an attitude, he’s out. No questions asked.”"
- "But the approach, though well‑intentioned, was crushing my son’s spirit."
