That is a real advance over "offer five minutes of presence", because it removes the parent's main failure mode, which is reading silence as their own failure. It then disappears. Chapter 8's rejected repair and Chapter 9's hesitant child are textbook red-zone cases, and neither chapter reaches for the tool that was built for exactly them.

Sources:
- "If your child is in the red zone, success may simply mean that you offered the space without demanding anything in return. You’re not trying to spark a conversation. You’re showing your child that when they are ready to talk, you are willing to listen."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Every worked example still assumes a parent home at the friction hour
nodes.description:
The concrete practices in Chapters 5-9 presuppose a specific material life: laying gear out the night before, a car ride to school, evening dishes, bedtime, and a three o'clock afternoon. The front matter recruits a parent with razor-thin margins and no village, but the examples are written for a parent physically present at the two highest-friction hours of a weekday. Shift work, a second job, split custody and a child in after-school care are not addressed.

The revision changes the inventory slightly without changing the pattern. Chapter 6's thirty-minutes-in-the-living-room-after-pickup example is gone with the "resting in view" material, and the replacement SMART goal is more portable — five minutes during the drive home, after dinner, or before bed. But Chapter 5's new opening runs the other way: the Tuesday water bottle scene assumes a parent doing a three-child school run, and the fix is putting the bottle by the door the night before. Chapter 6's new opening assumes a parent who can stop the exit routine to search for a book, and who drives past the school at recess.

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The book is most credible exactly where it downgrades its own claim — "it changed the tone"
nodes.description:
The shoes-by-the-door family is the only outcome in Chapters 5-9 reported with its limits attached: the intervention did not fix the morning, it changed how the morning felt. That is a modest, plausible, and checkable claim, and it is more persuasive than any of the transformation stories around it precisely because it declines to overreach. It also names the method's real dependent variable. Chapters 5-9 cannot actually deliver behaviour change on a two-minute budget, but they can plausibly deliver a shift in emotional tone — and where the book says so plainly it stops needing the reader's goodwill to carry the argument.

Sources:
- "Placing shoes and backpacks by the door the night before and checking in gently the next morning didn't change everything, but it changed the tone."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Across all five chapters the child is a nervous system to be read, never a party with obligations
nodes.description:
In Chapters 5-9 the parent anticipates, withholds correction, absorbs rejection, regulates first, paces the return, and adjusts the time and mode. The child's only assigned move in the entire span is the single modelled line in the repair conversation, "Next time, you can say 'I need space.'" That asymmetry is defensible for a six-year-old and is the book's honest reading of who can regulate whom. It is much harder to defend for the fourteen-year-olds the book keeps invoking, and the book never argues for it — the reciprocity question simply never comes up, which leaves the parent of a teenager without a principled place to stop absorbing.

Sources:
- "You model a new path. “Next time, you can say ‘I need space.’”"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The 2/5/2 budget behaves as a purchase price, not a dosage — Chapter 9 lets it shrink without limit
nodes.description:
Chapters 5-7 each open with a time commitment, and Chapter 7 closes by declaring the loop shut: "You are now living the full 9 minutes." Chapter 9 then permits the whole thing to collapse to ten seconds of dropped shoulders or a plate of apples pushed across the table, with no claim that the reduced version does less. If the nine minutes were a dose, shrinking it would cost something and the book would say what. Since nothing is forfeited, the number is doing recruitment work — it makes the method affordable to a reader who has already been told her margins are razor-thin — and the practice it names is really "any repeated intentional contact", which is a weaker and more honest claim.

Sources:
- "This third touchpoint closes the loop, bringing the whole rhythm back around. You are now living the full 9 minutes of the RootedInGood™ Method."
- "That might mean taking a single, deep breath in the car right before school pickup, or dropping your shoulders for ten seconds while you're standing at the kitchen counter."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Chapters 10-12 build a progress test that no outcome can fail
nodes.description:
Chapter 10 says the evidence of change is "incredibly easy to miss," Chapter 11 says you may not notice it all at once, and Chapter 12 says you are planting seeds you cannot see. Taken together these three chapters remove every state of the world in which a reader could conclude the method is not working: visible improvement confirms it, invisible improvement confirms it, and no improvement means you have not looked closely enough or waited long enough. This is reassuring and it is also epistemically empty — the book never names a single observation that would count as disconfirmation. The cost lands on the one reader the book most wants to help: the parent whose child is genuinely not responding has no sanctioned way to read that fact.

Sources:
- "These moments are incredibly easy to miss. But they are everything."
- "You may not notice it all at once. But if you stay with it, you begin to feel a solid foundation settling in underneath the noise."
- "You’re planting seeds you might not see yet, but they’re already taking root."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The book has an off-ramp for a depleted parent and none for a non-responding child
nodes.description:
The only referral guidance in the manuscript sits in Chapter 2 and in the front-matter disclaimer, and both are about the adult — a depleted nervous system, numbness, irritability, being unable to come back down. Nothing in Chapters 8 through 13 tells a parent what sustained non-response from the child might mean or when it warrants assessment, which is striking given that the author's own origin story is a child who did not respond to standard strategies and that she runs a behavioural treatment centre. The final content chapter is a confidence-builder and the closing line is "Return anyway," so the book's terminal instruction to a parent seeing nothing after a year is to keep doing the same thing. A single paragraph in Chapter 11 or 12 — what it looks like when the rhythm is holding but something else is also going on — would cost the book nothing and would close its largest safety gap.

Sources:
- "Reaching out to your doctor, therapist, partner, or a trusted friend is not a weakness. It is wisdom."
- "Some days may even feel like you’re taking steps backwards. Return anyway."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The SMART goal disappears after Chapter 9, right where measurement would test the method
nodes.description:
SMART appears in Chapters 5, 6 and 9 as the book's only instrument with an observable criterion — backpack and water bottle by the door for five school mornings. It vanishes entirely from Chapters 10 through 13, which replace it with interoception ("what does your body notice"), subtle-sign hunting, and trust in an unseen foundation. So the book supplies a measurable tool during the build phase and withdraws it at exactly the point where a reader would use it to ask whether the build worked. Whether this is deliberate protection of a fragile reader or an unexamined drift, the effect is that the outcome chapters are unauditable by the book's own earlier standard.

Sources:
- "What does your body notice when you intentionally open up half a second of space before responding?"
- "Intentionally stop waiting for a massive turnaround in your relationship. Watch for the tiny, fleeting signs of progress instead"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The 20-second touch finding comes from adult partner hugs, and the book's own reference says so
nodes.description:
Chapter 13 cites Light et al. (2005) for the claim that 20 seconds of physical touch significantly reduces physiological stress markers, and the reference list prints the study's actual subject: "More frequent partner hugs and higher oxytocin levels are linked to lower blood pressure and heart rate." That is a study of adult romantic partners, mostly premenopausal women, and it is a correlational blood-pressure finding rather than a dose-response result for a 20-second hug. The book has already built a named practice on the number — Chapter 7's 20-second hug, counted aloud — so the citation is load-bearing for a parent-child intervention it does not actually cover. Swapping in Feldman's parent-child synchrony work, already in the reference list, would cost one sentence and fix it.

Sources:
- "Research from the University of North Carolina found that as little as 20 seconds of physical touch can significantly reduce physiological stress markers (Light et al., 2005)."
- "Light, K. C., et al. (2005). More frequent partner hugs and higher oxytocin levels are linked to lower blood pressure and heart rate."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The bonus chapter evidences the three ingredients and never once evidences the nine minutes
nodes.description:
Every citation in Chapter 13 supports a general construct — scaffolding, attunement, oxytocin, social safety — and not one supports the specific structure the book actually sells: three touchpoints, daily, at two, five and two minutes. The 2/5/2 split is the trademarked, memorable, purchasable part of the method and it is the only part with no research behind it, yet the chapter's opening sentence treats it as the thing being validated. This is the classic move of borrowing the credibility of a literature for a protocol the literature never tested. The honest version is available and would still be persuasive: the ingredients are well evidenced, the dosage is the author's clinical judgement from twenty years of homes.

Sources:
- "You’ve seen how just 9 minutes a day can shift the emotional tone of your relationship with your child."
- "Each touchpoint in the RootedInGood™ Method is backed by science and designed for real life."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The one claim readers actually doubt — that early help breeds dependence — is the least evidenced
nodes.description:
Chapter 5 raises the objection in the reader's own voice, "if I keep stepping in, won't they stop trying?", and defers the answer to the science. Chapter 13 answers it with a Rooted Anchor assertion, Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (a theoretical frame, not a finding), and "antecedent strategies" with no citation attached. The one cited study, Blair and Raver 2015, is a school-readiness and self-regulation review whose interventions are classroom curricula, not two minutes of pre-emptive parental help. So the chapter that exists to supply rigour supplies the least of it at precisely the claim a skeptical parent brought with them.

Sources:
- "Helping early doesn’t prevent independence. It builds the internal safety needed to develop it."
- "In behaviour science, this aligns with what are called antecedent strategies, adjusting the environment or expectations before behaviour escalates"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Chapter 13's recap upgrades correlational findings into "clinical data" the disclaimer disowns
nodes.description:
The front matter says the method is not a substitute for medical, psychological or therapeutic care, but Chapter 13 tells the parent their tiny everyday actions are "backed by clinical data," instructs them to notice "the clinical shift in your child's posture," and claims touch "literally changes your child's brain and body chemistry." None of the cited work is clinical trial data on this method, and Denham 2003 is explicitly reported in the body as a correlation before the recap restates it as "Attunement is biological." The drift is one-directional — every restatement is stronger than the sentence it summarizes — which is the signature of a recap written to reassure rather than to compress. Since the recaps are what a tired parent actually rereads, the strongest claims in the book are the least supervised ones.

Sources:
- "How does knowing that your tiny, everyday actions are backed by clinical data settle your own nervous system today?"
- "Notice the clinical shift in your child's posture when you withhold correction and simply hold space."
- "Studies show that perceived parental attunement and responsiveness are directly correlated with higher emotional intelligence in children (Denham et al., 2003)."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Chapter 11's seven families are aged 7 to 14, mildly distant, and none of them are the origin child
nodes.description:
The vignette ages are 7, 9, 9 and 11, 10, 10, 14 and high school. Nobody is under seven — which is exactly the band Chapter 3 says needs the most borrowed regulation, since self-regulation "rarely arrives before age 7 or 8" — and nobody has a diagnosis, a school exclusion, a violent episode, or the kind of struggle that "didn't respond to traditional strategies" and produced the method in the first place. The presenting problems are quietness, volume, sensitivity to correction, sibling friction, and teenage drift. The author's stated specialism is neurodivergent children and her own hardest case is the book's origin, yet the evidence chapter of lived outcomes quietly selects the mildest population available.

Sources:
- "“We Weren’t Fighting. We Just Weren’t Close.” (Parent of a 9-year-old)"
- "There wasn’t anything extreme happening. Just tension. Back-and-forth."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Chapter 11 admits its stories are composites, then selects every one of them on a happy ending
nodes.description:
The chapter is honest about its evidentiary status — these are "reflections shaped by patterns I've witnessed," not case records — and that honesty is worth crediting. But seven composites authored by the method's owner, every one of which ends in a child returning, is selection on the dependent variable by construction: the pattern being illustrated is the pattern that was used to build the composites. The chapter even pre-empts the objection by noting nobody became perfect and some nearly quit, which grants imperfection of degree while conceding nothing about direction. A single composite that ends in a household still stuck after a year would cost the chapter little and would make the other six mean something.

Sources:
- "What follows are reflections shaped by patterns I’ve witnessed in homes doing this work. These are not fairy tales."
- "If you read these stories closely, you’ll notice something. No life became perfect. No child transformed overnight. What changed was the presence in the room."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Making the parent the only variable leaves only one place to assign a failure
nodes.description:
The method's central strength — you control your own nervous system, so start there — carries a structural cost the book never acknowledges. If the parent is the only lever, then a child who does not change implies a parent who did not regulate, and Chapter 11 reinforces this by resolving its two hardest cases inward: Mark's problem turns out to be his own volume, Ryan's turns out to be his own hope. Against that causal model the front matter's "You are not failing" is a mood, not an argument, and a reader who has practiced for months without movement will find the book has handed her the blame while withholding permission to feel it. Naming even one cause outside the parent's regulation — a sensory profile, a school placement, a sibling, a grief — would break the trap without weakening the method.

Sources:
- "“It’s not that he’s easier,” Mark said later. “I just stopped bringing the storm into the room.”"
- "In that moment, the distance wasn’t in his actions. It was in his hope."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Every second adult in the book cooperates, so the unsupportive co-parent case is never modelled
nodes.description:
The front matter rules the co-parent out of scope, and then the book quietly stocks itself with co-parents who make that easy: Chapter 10's partner "could handle the details just as thoughtfully as I could," Chapter 4's husband agrees with the decision to pull their son off the team, Chapter 10's Try This invites the reader to hand a moment to "your partner or your children." The only adult who actively damages a child is the basketball coach — someone outside the household, whom the family can exit. The scope limit is defensible as an anti-goal but it is not tested anywhere, so a reader whose partner mocks the nine minutes, contradicts the boundary an hour later, or is the source of the child's dysregulation gets no sentence written for her, and Chapter 10's instruction to leave a space open is actively risky in that home.

Sources:
- "It is not about correcting your co-parent."
- "My partner could handle the details just as thoughtfully as I could. My children each carried their own strengths."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Chapter 10 infers "step back and capability appears" from one household that already had it
nodes.description:
The chapter's whole claim rests on a single vignette in which the author stops jumping in and discovers a thoughtful spouse and children with their own strengths. Her own sentence concedes the mechanism — pausing "allowed me to see the ability and steadiness that were already there" — which means the finding is about her perception, not about what pausing produces in a household where the ability is not yet there. Transposed to a solo parent, to younger children, or to a genuinely unsafe sibling dynamic, "leave an open logistical or emotional space today" produces a dropped ball rather than a revealed strength. The guard against this is one sentence, has no criterion attached, and arrives as reassurance rather than as a rule for when to fill the space instead.

Sources:
- "Pausing didn’t make the people in my home suddenly capable; it allowed me to see the ability and steadiness that were already there."
- "Intentionally leave an open logistical or emotional space today. Let your partner or your children step up and manage a moment on their own terms."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Chapter 12's payoff is a child skill the book spends thirteen chapters never teaching
nodes.description:
The stated end state is a son who "can feel himself beginning to rise out of his window of tolerance" and can pause — interoceptive self-monitoring plus a self-initiated regulation move. The phrase "window of tolerance" appears exactly once in the manuscript, undefined, on that line. Chapter 2's 5-point awareness scale is the only mapping instrument in the book and it is explicitly for the adult; nothing anywhere is addressed to the child, gives the child language, or describes teaching the child to name a level. The book's theory is that the skill transfers by exposure to a regulated adult, which is a real developmental claim, but it is never stated as a claim and never evidenced, so the terminal outcome arrives as a gift rather than as anything the reader is equipped to build toward.

Sources:
- "He can feel himself beginning to rise out of his window of tolerance. He can pause. And when he can’t, I wait."
- "Below is a 5-point scale I use with families to map out these internal shifts."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Every child who refuses contact in this book relents, so sustained refusal has no playbook
nodes.description:
Rejection recurs across Chapters 7, 8, 9 and 11 — the son who pushed her away, the repair that is refused, Maya's "why do you have to make everything a thing?", Aaron's three days of silence — and in every instance it is a beat inside an arc that resolves. The advice for refusal is therefore calibrated to temporary refusal: pace the return in layers, hovering counts, press play. None of that is falsifiable at any duration, so a parent two years into a child who will not be touched, will not be driven anywhere, and will not answer a text is told the same thing as a parent three days in. This is the most consequential untested case in the book, and it is the one a reader in real trouble most likely bought it for.

Sources:
- "He didn’t respond that day. Or the next. On the third day, he texted back: “Fine.”"
- "The connection didn’t look like it used to. But it held."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The nine-minute promise is priced in minutes and paid in months, and Chapter 11 does the arithmetic
nodes.description:
Chapter 11's own timestamps are three weeks for Julia, the second month for Mark, mid-year for Alisha, three months before Ryan sees anything, and months later for Aaron; Chapter 9 adds the hug that took over a year. The real ask is therefore nine minutes a day sustained across a multi-month stretch with no feedback, which is a completely different commitment from nine minutes and a far harder one — sustaining an unrewarded behaviour is exactly what the book's own behaviour-science chapter would predict people fail at. The book never states this total anywhere, and it is not a weakness of the method but of the marketing of it. Saying "plan on three months before you see anything" up front would set the expectation that Chapters 10 to 12 then have to spend themselves repairing.

Sources:
- "By month three, nothing looked noticeably different."
- "“I feel like I’m putting in all this effort,” he said, “and he doesn’t even notice.”"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Chapter 10 refusing to assign homework is the book's sharpest structural move, and it is easy to miss
nodes.description:
Self-help books fail in a predictable way: the reader who is not seeing results adds more technique, the load rises, the practice collapses, and the collapse is read as personal failure. Chapter 10 blocks that path by spending an entire chapter adding nothing — no fourth touchpoint, no new script, and an explicit refusal of a fresh homework assignment — and it pairs with Chapter 9's "press play, not restart" and the principle that connection is not a checklist item to put "do more, harder" formally out of bounds. Placing it directly before the payoff chapters is also correct sequencing, since it lowers the stakes before the testimonials raise them. It is the least showy chapter in the book and the one doing the most structural work.

Sources:
- "So let’s leave this chapter right here, not with a fresh homework assignment, but with permission to just trust what’s already there."
- "Connection is not a checklist item. Deep bonds aren't built by doing more."

Regenerate a PDF or ship a redline change list instead
Deliver rooted-v2.docx so the author restyles in her own Google Doc

Words are only one source of information, so behaviour has to be read
nodes.description:
The observational premise the author brought from behaviour analysis into parenting, and the mechanism that makes curiosity necessary rather than merely kind. A dysregulated child may not have access to language that explains what is happening for them, so the adult who waits for an accurate verbal account will wait a long time. This is the front matter's warrant for reading behaviour as information.

Sources:
- "I learned that words are only one source of information. When a child is overwhelmed, upset, or dysregulated, they may not have access to the words that accurately explain what is happening for them."
- "To look for patterns. To ask what might be happening beneath behaviour instead of reacting only to what I could see."
- "careful observation can help us look beneath what we see and beyond what we hear, before deciding what it means."

nodes.title: The five questions the author asks before deciding what a behaviour means
nodes.description:
Curiosity is given a procedure rather than left as an attitude. Four of the five questions are about context and contingency — what came before, what changed after, what the child moves toward or away from, what brings relief — and the fifth turns the instrument on the observer. Together they are the front matter's working definition of getting curious.

Sources:
- "What happened before this? What changed afterward? What does this child move toward or away from? What seems to bring relief? What am I missing?"
- "So I learned to get curious."

nodes.title: The ordinary moments that turned out to be building something: the car, the bed edge, the kitchen
nodes.description:
The revision supplies the concrete content of connection, which the earlier draft asserted but never itemised. Four unremarkable moments are named, and the claim attached to them is specifically about scale: each is small enough to be missed, and the effect is cumulative rather than individual. This is where the book's unit of work gets set.

Sources:
- "I began paying closer attention to the ordinary moments that didn't look particularly important at the time."
- "A conversation in the car. Sitting on the edge of a bed for a few extra minutes. A hug in the kitchen. Putting something down long enough to really listen."
- "These moments were small enough to miss. But together, they were building something."

nodes.title: The mentorship lineage: Klein, Coulson, Ryan and Carbone, and a habit of learning across disciplines
nodes.description:
The revised bio grounds the author's expertise in named people rather than in years served. Two early mentors are credited with shaping her understanding of data, reinforcement and measurement, and two further leaders were later brought into the centre to train her staff. The bio also claims breadth deliberately — speech-language pathologists, occupational therapists, psychologists, physicians and educators — which is what licenses the book's move of looking outside behaviour for an explanation.

Sources:
- "Among them were Dr. Gerard Klein, Under the Umbrella Tree's longtime consulting clinical psychologist, and Dr. Grant Coulson, whose mentorship helped shape her early understanding of data, reinforcement, and careful measurement."
- "She built close collaborations with speech-language pathologists, occupational therapists, psychologists, physicians, educators, and other professionals who expanded the way she understood children and the environments around them."
- "As Under the Umbrella Tree grew, Lolly also brought respected leaders in the field- including Bob Ryan, Dr. Vincent Carbone, and later Dr. Coulson himself-into the centre to provide intensive training to her team."

nodes.title: The reach argument: train one professional and the effect compounds through everyone they go on to serve
nodes.description:
The revised bio's answer to the scale question, and its reason for counting something other than children seen. More than twenty people who trained at the centre became clinicians or founded businesses; the practitioners and educators she taught carried the work into rooms she will never enter. The bio concedes the number is unquantifiable and argues the direction anyway.

Sources:
- "More than twenty of the people who learned and developed at Under the Umbrella Tree have gone on to become clinicians, build businesses of their own, or both."
- "The number is impossible to quantify, but the ripple effect is not: investing in one professional can influence the children and families they go on to support throughout their own career."
- "Her team's research has been presented at the Ontario Association for Behaviour Analysis (ONTABA), and she has lectured and spoken at York University's Seneca campus."

nodes.title: The inversion the bio turns on: the one who asked the questions became the one who gets called
nodes.description:
The revised bio's narrative arc, and the source of its claim to authority. The young clinician who sought out experienced people and asked constantly becomes the person other clinicians call when they need a second read on a pattern. The bio converts that into an obligation rather than a status, and states it as the principle the book is written under.

Sources:
- "The young professional who once sought out experienced clinicians and asked endless questions became the clinician other clinicians began calling when they needed another perspective, help seeing a pattern they might be missing, or simply someone they trusted to think a difficult situation through with them."
- "She believes there is a responsibility that comes with experience: You pass it on."
- "RootedInGood™ brings that same spirit of curiosity to parenting."

nodes.title: Get curious: look underneath the behaviour, and then underneath your own reaction to it
nodes.description:
The revision's replacement for the Personal Note's old control-versus-trying-harder framing, and the larger of the two moves the section now makes. Curiosity arrives first as a professional discipline learned before motherhood, then is turned a second time on the parent themselves when the author's own child stops responding to what she already knows. The doubling is the point: understanding the child is explicitly named as only part of the work.

Sources:
- "So I learned to get curious."
- "I had to become curious again. Not only about my child, but about myself."
- "What was activating me? What expectations was I bringing into difficult moments? What patterns was I repeating without realizing it? What was happening between us?"
- "We have to be willing to understand ourselves too."

nodes.title: The kindergarten lunchroom: two administrators with walkie-talkies, and they couldn't catch him
nodes.description:
The revision's new opening scene, and the book's most concrete picture of the behaviour it is trying to explain. The author is called to the school and walks into a lunchroom where two administrators are coordinating by radio how to catch her son as he runs across the tabletops. The scene is left unresolved on purpose — they couldn't — and it is deliberately unreadable at this point in the chapter, because the chapter's argument is that the visible behaviour was never the information.

Sources:
- "I still remember a call I received from his school when he was in kindergarten. I needed to come immediately."
- "When I arrived, I walked into the lunchroom to find an administrator at each end, walkie-talkies in hand, trying to coordinate how they were going to catch my son as he ran across the tops of the tables."
- "They couldn't."

nodes.title: The harder part came after: his account of events didn't match what the adults had seen
nodes.description:
The revision names something the earlier draft never did — that the aftermath was worse than the incident. The son's account of what had happened could be completely disconnected from what the adults around him witnessed, and the author rules out the obvious explanation immediately: he was not lying, and what he believed felt entirely real to him. That leaves her with a problem no behaviour strategy addresses, which is how to help him reconstruct an event without telling him his experience of it was false.

Sources:
- "As difficult as those moments were, what came afterward could be even harder. I would listen as he tried to tell me what had happened, and sometimes his understanding of the situation seemed completely disconnected from what the adults around him had witnessed."
- "He wasn't lying. What he believed had happened felt completely real to him."
- "I had to learn how to help him piece together what had happened without dismissing what had felt completely real to him."

nodes.title: The thing nobody was looking for: he lacked peripheral vision in his left eye
nodes.description:
The revision's resolution, and it arrives from outside behaviour entirely. A vision deficit no one had been looking for turned out to be contributing substantially to what everyone was seeing, and once the eye was treated the behaviour acquired context. The chapter is careful with the claim — the explanation is partial, not total, and it does not retroactively make the author negligent. It is the book's proof case that visible behaviour and the reason for it can be very far apart.

Sources:
- "Eventually, we discovered something none of us had been looking for: he lacked peripheral vision in his left eye. Once his eye was treated, we began to understand just how much that had been contributing to what we were seeing."
- "Suddenly, some of the behaviour that had seemed so difficult to explain had context."
- "I knew enough professionally to understand that behaviour rarely tells us the whole story. But knowing that and figuring out what was happening with my own child were two very different things."

nodes.title: Recap principle: behaviour doesn't always tell us the whole story
nodes.description:
A fourth bullet the revision adds to the Chapter 1 recap, and the one that carries the new opening material. It states the lunchroom-and-eye story as a general rule: what is visible is information, not explanation, and the work is staying curious about what may sit underneath it. The chapter closes by returning to the boy on the tables to make the same point narratively.

Sources:
- "Behaviour doesn't always tell us the whole story. What we see on the outside is information, but understanding often requires us to stay curious about what may be happening underneath."
- "In many ways, that brings us back to the little boy running across those lunchroom tables."
- "The behaviour was impossible to miss. What was underneath it was much harder to see. And that is where this work begins."

nodes.title: The pep talk that never worked: remember what we talked about, keep your body calm, make good choices
nodes.description:
The revision's new opening for Chapter 3, and the chapter's diagnostic scene. Before every birthday party or sporting event the author gave her son the same encouraging pre-brief, he agreed to it sincerely, and it failed anyway once the room got loud and his body moved faster than his thinking. The scene is set up so neither party is at fault: he was not making a promise he intended to break, and she was not failing to prepare him.

Sources:
- "For years, before almost every birthday party, sporting event, or situation I knew might be difficult for my son, I would give him the pep talk."
- "Remember what we talked about. Keep your body calm. Listen. Make good choices."
- "He wasn't making a promise he intended to break. He meant it. And so did I."
- "The excitement would get too big. The room would get too loud. Something wouldn't go the way he expected. His body would start moving faster than his thinking."

nodes.title: The error the chapter names: confusing knowing with doing
nodes.description:
The revision's central new concept, and the thing the pep talks were getting wrong. Because the son could recite the rules when calm, the author treated the skill as mastered and expected it to be available anywhere, at any time, under any conditions. The chapter's correction is that knowing what to do while regulated and being able to reach it while overwhelmed are different capacities. The skill was not missing; access to it was.

Sources:
- "I was confusing knowing with doing."
- "Because he could tell me the rules, I assumed the skill was mastered. In my mind, we had taught it, talked about it, practised it, and he understood it. So when the moment came, I expected him to be able to use it. Anywhere. At any time. Under any conditions."
- "But knowing what to do while calm and being able to do it when your nervous system is overwhelmed are two very different things."
- "The skill wasn't gone. He just couldn't always reach it when he needed it most."

nodes.title: Stop asking why he isn't doing what he knows, and start asking what is getting in the way
nodes.description:
The question-swap the revision builds the chapter around, and the practical consequence of separating knowing from doing. The first question treats the gap as motivational and produces more reminders; the second treats it as a question about conditions and produces observation. The author reports acting on it directly: fewer pre-party briefings, more watching for what happened just before things came apart.

Sources:
- "Once I understood that, I stopped asking myself: Why isn't he doing what he knows? And I started asking a different question: What is getting in the way of him using what he knows right now?"
- "That question changed everything."
- "I stopped giving so many pre-party and pre-game pep talks. And I started watching. Not watching for him to mess up. Watching for what happened before he did."

nodes.title: The glance across the room: co-regulation turned out to be less, not more
nodes.description:
The resolution of the revision's new opening, and its most economical statement of what co-regulation costs. Watching instead of briefing, the author noticed her son was also watching her — finding her eyes across a busy room for a second at a time. What he needed at that moment was not another reminder of the rules but a smile or a thumbs-up, after which he returned to what he was doing. The chapter draws the conclusion explicitly: this was not another thing to add.

Sources:
- "And then I noticed something else. He was watching me too. Across a busy room, his eyes would find mine. Sometimes it lasted only a second."
- "And when he found me, he didn't need another reminder of the rules. He didn't need me to come over and pull him aside for another talk."
- "Sometimes it wasn't another reminder. It was a glance across the room. A smile. A thumbs-up. A tiny bit of support at the moment he needed it."
- "Co-regulation wasn't another thing I had to add. Sometimes, it was actually less."

nodes.title: It was Tuesday: the failure point was predictable and she already knew where it was
nodes.description:
The realisation the revision builds the chapter's premise on, and the reason Focused Support is described as noticing rather than helping. Once her own system settled, the author could see that nothing about the morning had been a surprise: it was Tuesday, he had practice, they were always rushing, and remembering his gear on those mornings was reliably hard for him. The question that follows is not why he forgot but why she hadn't acted on what she already knew.

Sources:
- "And once my own system settled, one thought kept coming back to me: I knew this was going to happen."
- "It was Tuesday. He had practice. We were almost always rushing. And remembering everything he needed on those mornings was hard for him."
- "So why hadn't I just gotten the water bottle?"
- "But because I already knew where the morning was likely to fall apart."

nodes.title: The belief that had to be dismantled: helping too much means you are parenting wrong
nodes.description:
The internal objection the chapter has to clear before the touchpoint is usable, and the revision states it as an absorbed message rather than a considered position. If he is old enough to remember the water bottle, she should expect him to remember the water bottle. The chapter's answer does not concede the developmental point — she can still teach him to pack, still expect responsibility, still work toward independence — it only refuses the timing. A rushed Tuesday morning with three children is not the moment to insist on it.

Sources:
- "Somewhere along the way, I had absorbed the message that helping too much meant I was somehow doing parenting wrong. If he was old enough to remember his water bottle, then surely I should expect him to remember his water bottle."
- "I could still teach him to pack for practice. I could still expect him to take responsibility. I could still work toward independence."
- "But Tuesday morning, when three kids were trying to get out the door and we were already running late, wasn't the moment to insist he do it on his own."

nodes.title: Put the water bottle by the door: two minutes, not forever, just for now
nodes.description:
The chapter's concrete resolution, and the shape every act of Focused Support is meant to take. The intervention is trivially small and explicitly temporary, and the revision attaches both qualifiers deliberately — the help is bounded in time and in duration, which is what separates it from rescuing. The principle drawn out of it reframes independence as something built by timing rather than by withholding.

Sources:
- "Maybe I could put the water bottle by the door. Two minutes. Maybe less. Not forever. Just for now."
- "What if helping him before we reached that moment wasn't doing too much? What if it was simply noticing sooner?"
- "Because independence isn't built by repeatedly watching a child struggle with something we already know is hard for them."
- "Sometimes, it begins with knowing when to step in—and when to step back."

nodes.title: The Harry Potter book: a Grade 2 boy who could not leave the house without it
nodes.description:
The revision's new opening for Chapter 6, and the chapter's whole argument in narrative form. After starting a new school, the author's son became hyper-vigilant about taking his Harry Potter book with him. The book itself was unremarkable — he was an early reader — but the need for it was not, and one morning he could not find it and panicked. The revision marks the distinction carefully: this was not annoyance at a missing book. Something about his face stopped her from delivering any of the reasonable lines she had available.

Sources:
- "He had become hyper-vigilant about bringing his Harry Potter book to school. Every day."
- "He was an early reader and had taken to the Harry Potter series very young, so seeing him with one of those big novels tucked under his arm wasn't unusual. But the way he needed that book with him was."
- "Not I'm annoyed because I can't find my book upset. Panicked."
- "We were trying to get out the door. There were things to do. Places to be. And I could easily have said: We'll find it later. You don't need it today. You're going to be late."
- "But something about the look on his face stopped me. This was about more than a book."

nodes.title: Detective mode: ask a little, listen a lot, and give it a week
nodes.description:
What the author actually did with the Harry Potter signal, and the revision's working definition of Intentional Listening as an investigation rather than a conversation. She began asking about the book that evening, explicitly not interrogating, and got nothing that night. It took roughly a week of paying attention and leaving enough room for him to feel comfortable. The chapter's point is the ratio and the timescale: asking a little, listening a lot, and not requiring the answer on the first attempt.

Sources:
- "I went into detective mode. That evening, I started asking about the book. Not interrogating. Not demanding an answer. Just getting curious."
- "I didn't get the answer that night. In fact, it took about a week."
- "A week of paying attention. A week of asking a little and listening a lot. A week of giving him enough space to feel comfortable telling me what was really happening."

nodes.title: The story underneath the story: he was being bullied at his new school
nodes.description:
The disclosure the week of listening produced, and the payoff of the revision's new opening. He had not been able to come downstairs and say he was having a hard time at his new school; what he could give her was a request for a book. The chapter reads the whole sequence as a translation problem rather than a concealment one, and it retroactively explains the panic. Note what the disclosure turns out to be: the revision now has a worked example in which non-directive listening surfaces bullying.

Sources:
- "And eventually, the story underneath the story began to come out. He was being bullied by another child in his class."
- "Suddenly, that frantic morning made sense."
- "He hadn't known how to come downstairs and say: Mom, I'm having a hard time at my new school."
- "He said: I need my Harry Potter book. And for a while, that was the only part of the story he could give me."

nodes.title: Core principle: listening begins before the words do
nodes.description:
The revision's new organising claim for Chapter 6, extracted from the Harry Potter story and repeated at the chapter's close. Listening is not defined as the reception of speech; the first thing a child offers may be a behaviour, a question, a change in routine, or an object they suddenly cannot leave without. This imports the front matter's behaviour-is-information premise directly into the listening touchpoint, and it is stated as a new recap bullet.

Sources:
- "Because listening isn't always about sitting across from your child while they tell you exactly what's wrong. Sometimes they can't."
- "Sometimes the first thing they give you is a behaviour. A question. A change in routine. A book they suddenly cannot leave the house without."
- "Sometimes listening begins before the words do."
- "Listening can begin before the words do. Changes in behaviour, routines, or the things your child suddenly seems to need may be invitations to become curious."

nodes.title: Editorial: Chapter 3 was supplied in two versions, and the later one was taken
nodes.description:
The rooted-edits manuscript contains Chapter 3 twice, the second headed "Chapter 3—with further edits (read both and decide)". The two are identical except in four places, and every difference runs the same direction: the later version removes hard developmental claims. "Around age 7 or 8" and "into the mid-twenties" become gradual development into early adulthood; "they don't actually know better yet" becomes a distinction between knowing and being able to access what you know; "misbehaviour is often a biological inability, not a choice" becomes a child who may know what is expected and still not reach it; and the moment a rhythm begins is loosened from a child who lets you share space to a child who experiences you as steady even when the closeness they need changes.

The later version was merged. It is the more defensible one — the earlier draft asserts specific neurodevelopmental timelines the book does not source, and states them as verdicts about individual children — and nothing of substance is lost, since the chapter's function is unchanged. The cost is the loss of a concrete age anchor that parents find memorable.

This choice is worth flagging to the author, because it is the only place in the merge where a judgement was made rather than a change applied.

nodes.title: Editorial: the revision's consistent direction is downgrading guarantees to tendencies
nodes.description:
Across all six revised sections the same edit is made repeatedly, independent of subject matter. Claims about what will happen become claims about what can happen. A sample: "they make a lasting impact" becomes "they can make"; "limits give them a sense of safety" becomes "limits can provide"; "they don't experience your limits as rejection, they experience them as protection" becomes "limits can be easier to hear and tolerate"; "what will make them start seeking you out" becomes "what can help them begin to"; "linked to stronger emotional health, improved behaviour, and greater long-term resilience" becomes "associated with stronger emotional well-being and healthier relationships"; "you set the tone" becomes "you help set the tone"; "You are not failing" becomes "chances are, you are doing far more than anyone sees".

Two consequences for the graph. Several outcome nodes are now weaker claims than their titles implied and have been retitled. And the alignment branch's tensions are mostly unaffected, because they concern structure rather than strength of claim — with the exception of the "You are not failing" promise, which no longer appears in the book in that form.

nodes.title: rooted-v2.docx: the merged manuscript, 13 chapters with the revisions applied
nodes.description:
The deliverable. rooted.pdf with every revision from rooted-edits.pdf merged in, written as a Word document so the author can re-import it into Google Docs and restyle there rather than accept a regenerated PDF.

What it contains: the copyright page and all front matter, the revised Personal Note and author bio, the three front-matter sections the edits did not touch, Chapter 1 and Chapters 3, 5 and 6 in their revised form, Chapters 2, 4 and 7-13 unchanged, and the References. About 30,600 words in 1,568 paragraphs, up from roughly 29,100.

Fidelity: real Heading 1/2 styles so the Google Docs outline survives the import; bold, italics, bullets and the Connection Spectrum emoji preserved; the 5-point awareness scale rebuilt as a proper Word table rather than the interleaved columns a PDF text extraction produces; all [ANCHOR] and [INSERT ILLUSTRATION PLACEHOLDER] markers carried through verbatim. rooted.pdf is untouched.

Known gap: the Table of Contents page numbers are stale, because the revised chapters run longer. The entries themselves are unchanged apart from Chapter 3, retitled from "Co-Regulation." to "Co-Regulation:" to match the revision.

nodes.title: Graph patched section by section: 24 nodes added, 4 deleted, 60 rewritten, every quote re-verified
nodes.description:
The graph now describes the merged manuscript rather than the original. Nodes for the front matter and Chapters 1, 3, 5 and 6 were rewritten or replaced; the nodes for Chapters 2, 4 and 7-13 were left alone because that text did not change.

Added: the curiosity origin and the mentorship lineage in the front matter; the lunchroom, the mismatched account and the peripheral vision discovery in Chapter 1; the pep talk, knowing-versus-doing and the glance across the room in Chapter 3; the Tuesday water bottle in Chapter 5; the Harry Potter book, detective mode and the bullying disclosure in Chapter 6.

Deleted: the four nodes for material the revision cut - resting in view, the laundry-pile vignette, the retreating-upstairs confession, and the outcome that hung off it.

Re-verified: every Sources quote in the graph was checked against the merged manuscript. 1,089 quotes across all 448 nodes now appear verbatim; the ones that had drifted were repointed to the current wording, and the ones whose source text was deleted were re-sourced from surviving passages.

Lolly dates the whole goal to this morning: it is where she saw she was escalating rather than co-regulating, and understood co-regulation begins in her own internal world.

The chapter attaches this caution directly to the goal, conceding regulation can feel impossible on a depleted system and directing the parent to outside support.

The Before kitchen scene is the autopilot option played out: instinct to yell, sharpened voice, the storm carried into the room.

Level 3 is the starred early warning on the scale, and the scale prescribes this move for it.

themes.name: connection-cushions-boundaries
themes.description: Warmth and limits are repeatedly refused as a trade-off: connection is what makes a hard no land as protection instead of rejection. Chapter 1 sets it up by rejecting both compliance-chasing and letting things slide, Chapter 2 answers the fear 'if I soften, will they still listen?', and Chapter 3 states the rule outright as connection before correction. Chapter 5 restates it as friction points being invitations rather than behaviours, Chapter 8 returns to the limit from calm, and Chapter 13 supplies the scaffolding research behind it.

themes.name: consistency-over-intensity
themes.description: Nine ordinary minutes, repeated, are claimed to outperform grand gestures, extra hours, or an overnight overhaul of how you parent. It begins in the front matter's refusal of 'more time' as the fix, structures Chapter 1's three touchpoints and micro-moment pivots, and governs Chapter 7's choice of an existing daily moment over a staged movie-moment. Chapter 9 protects it with tiny handshakes on hard days, Chapter 12 names consistency rather than perfection as what rebuilds the relationship, and Chapter 13 gives it the small-repeated-doses argument.

themes.name: meet-the-child-in-front-of-you
themes.description: Fairness is defined as responsiveness to actual need, and the method bends to the specific child rather than the child bending to the method. Chapter 1 chooses equity over equality and releases the guilt of counting equal minutes, Chapter 3 slows the pace for neurodivergent and sensitive children because the goal isn't speed but safety, and Chapter 4's basketball decision is made on what the son needed rather than what his mother wanted. Chapter 9 permits pivoting the time or mode entirely, and Chapter 11's Alisha and Maya test the same principle across siblings and a teenager who went quiet.

themes.name: parent-is-the-intervention
themes.description: The book's most load-bearing claim: the variable you actually control is the adult's nervous system, so every technique starts inside the parent rather than on the child. The front matter names it (intention, not tighter control), Chapter 2 makes it a precondition with the awareness scale and the thirty-second reset, Chapter 3 calls it a nervous-system loan, and Chapter 4 insists the child feels you before they hear you. It resurfaces in Chapter 8, where regulating yourself is the invisible first move of repair, and in Chapter 11's Mark, whose son's problem turned out to be his father's volume

themes.name: presence-over-the-right-words
themes.description: What a struggling child receives is posture, tone and proximity, not phrasing, so the book keeps trading scripts for a steadier body. Chapter 4 builds the whole case (be the steady thing rather than say the perfect thing; the Grade 3 teacher's wordless daily smile), Chapter 6 turns the parent from manager into witness who can simply rest in view, and Chapter 7 puts touch before language as the first move rather than the last resort. Chapter 1's mom beside the Lego and Chapter 13's closing line — science explains it, the relationship brings it to life — bracket the same point.

themes.name: progress-hides-in-the-ordinary
themes.description: The evidence that the work is working is small, slow and easy to dismiss, so the book keeps redefining what counts as proof and asking the parent to trust an unseen foundation. Chapter 7's unprompted hug after a year and Chapter 9's doubt, meme-texting parent and month of silence set the pattern; Chapter 10 is a deliberate pause purely to notice change that already happened. Chapter 11 reads progress as shorter arguments and a child who lingers rather than one dramatic breakthrough, and Chapter 12 closes on seeds you cannot see yet.

themes.name: repair-is-the-relationship
themes.description: Rupture is assumed, so the skill being taught is the return — not avoiding the blow-up but coming back afterwards, in layers, at whatever pace the child allows. Chapter 2 ends on noticing your state and finding your footing again, Chapter 8 is the full treatment (re-entry scripts, the five-move conversation, rejection and returning too soon), and Chapter 9 compresses it into 'press play, not restart.' Chapter 9 also extends repair to honesty about your own empty days, and Chapter 11 closes with a gentle return never being starting from scratch.

themes.name: restraint-is-an-action
themes.description: Not fixing is treated as the harder, more skilled move: holding space, waiting a beat longer, and leaving a gap the child can step into. Chapter 3 asks the parent to sit beside a crying child without stopping the tears, Chapter 6 rules out teaching, correcting and problem-solving during the listening window, and Chapter 10 is built almost entirely from it — stop, breathe, wait, leave one space unfilled. Chapter 12's 'wait' and Chapter 13's Be a Witness, Not a Manager give the same restraint a payoff and a mechanism.

themes.name: safety-before-teaching
themes.description: A dysregulated nervous system literally cannot receive a lesson, so bodily safety has to be restored before anything instructive is attempted. Chapter 2's awareness scale and Chapter 3's account of self-regulation arriving at seven or eight and maturing into the mid-twenties establish the physiology; Chapter 7 reads fight, flight, freeze and fawn as one signal and answers with proximity and the 20-second hug. Chapter 8 opens on survival mode as the reason correction in the heat fails, and Chapter 13 supplies the evidence — the Still Face Experiment, oxytocin, Polyvagal Theory, cortisol droppin

themes.name: support-grows-independence
themes.description: Stepping in early is argued to produce capability rather than dependence — independence is the result of support, not its absence. Chapter 5 makes it the central reframe, fielding the objection 'won't they stop trying?' and separating partnering from rescuing; Chapter 3 frames the same thing as borrowing the parent's strength until the child can stand alone. Chapter 10 finds capability the family already had once the parent stops filling the space, Chapter 12 turns trust in the parent into the child's trust in himself, and Chapter 13 backs it with antecedent strategies and the Zone of Proximal
